title: Attacking a castled king: count at the weak square

steps.text: To judge an attack on a castled king, **count at the weak square**: how many of your pieces attack it, and how many of his defend it, the king included. The weak square is usually part of the pawn cover, such as h2 or h7. More attackers than defenders is a reason to look further, not a proof.

steps.text: The count only helps if every counted piece really reaches the square: a piece standing in its way blocks a line and removes an attacker. Treat the count as a **rule of thumb** and check the move itself. In the next three positions the same queen sacrifice is tried after one small change.

steps.text: A king still in the centre is a target when lines can be opened toward him and his pieces cannot cover them in time. To attack him you need **open lines** and attackers that arrive first. steps.text: A direct attack is a commitment. After the first sacrifice you cannot take it back, and his replies are mostly forced. So **before** the first move, write the whole line, list every piece that must move or support, and check that each can arrive. The last piece to arrive often decides (a **rule of thumb**). If one piece cannot come, do not start yet.

title: The Greek gift: when the bishop sacrifice on h7 works, and when it does not

steps.text: The **Greek gift** is the bishop sacrifice on h7 (or h2). Bxh7+ Kxh7 drags the king out; then the knight checks from g5 and the queen joins on h5. It asks for a bishop on the b1-h7 diagonal, a knight that can reach g5, and a queen (or another piece) that can join on h5. It is a pattern with conditions, not a trick that always works.

steps.caption: White to move. Only the black king defends h7, and the bishop on c1 guards g5.

The queen joins. Two white pieces now attack h7 and one black piece defends it.
Black takes the knight with the queen.
The bishop takes the queen.

Along the engine's best-defence line White ends at least 2 points ahead.

Only the king defends h7.

steps.text: Check these before you play it, as a **rule of thumb**: the bishop reaches h7 with check; a knight can check from g5 and no black piece can safely take it (a bishop on e7 can; a queen can if g5 is unguarded); a queen can join on h5; no black knight on f6 covers h7. If one is missing the sacrifice may lose a piece. The engine check decides.

title: How fast to attack: forcing now or calm first
outcomes: Chooses between forcing play now and a calm strengthening move, and gives the reason (king in the centre, or sound cover)
Explains why a calm move that adds an attacker is not passive
Tests whether a defender's piece already in place changes the right pace
Recognises a position with no attack to pace because material is simply free

steps.text:
How fast should an attack go? Two speeds.
**Quick:** forcing moves now (checks, captures, sacrifices), because the king is still in the centre or the defenders are not yet near.
**Moderate:** a calm move that brings one more piece to bear, because forcing moves would only trade your attackers away.
A calm move that adds an attacker is not passive.

steps.caption: Black to move. White's king is still on e1 and has not castled.

line.say: Check at once, while the king is still in the centre.
White takes the bishop with the queen.
The knight takes the queen.

claims.statement: Bxf2+ is the engine's best move.
Along the engine line Bxf2+ nets Black at least 4 points.
The white king is in the centre.
The calm Qd5 is far worse.

steps.text: **Moderate pace.** When the king is sheltered behind pawns, forcing moves often run out of pieces. A calm move that adds one more attacker can beat a check. Ask: which of my pieces is not yet attacking? This is a *rule of thumb*. Whether to attack at all is the lesson 'Count before you attack: attack now, not yet, or no'.

**Conditions.** Quick when the king is still in the centre or open files point at it. Moderate when the king is sheltered and you can add an attacker.
**Fails.** A slow move while the king can still castle gives him time. A calm plan fails when the defender's piece is already in place: test that before trusting the plan.

steps.text: A **pawn storm** pushes pawns at a castled king to open a file or diagonal for your pieces. It belongs mainly to **opposite-side castling**, where pawns are cheap and speed counts. A **lever** is a pawn move that attacks one of the pawns shielding the king. Before pushing, count the pieces standing ready behind the pawns.

steps.caption: Black to move. g4 is a lever (it attacks the shield pawn on h3), but a lever is not yet a good move: the engine prefers Nxd3.

The pawn moves after which the moved pawn attacks h3 are exactly g4.

steps.text: **Conditions.** A storm works when many of your pieces can join before the defender's pieces arrive, and the pawn barrier can be broken. It fails when the barrier is intact and defenders are near. Finding a lever does not tell you whether to play it. *Rule of thumb:* the side that opens lines first often has the initiative, but that is not a theorem. Call a storm *practical* unless you calculated it to be *sound*.

title: Count before you attack: attack now, not yet, or no

steps.text: An attack needs **tangible superiority** at its target: more of your pieces bear on it than he can bring to defend it, and his own threats are not faster. So count: the pieces that attack the target, those that can join in a move, then his defenders. The count is a **rule of thumb**: it tells you where to look, and the move still has to be checked.

steps.text: Three verdicts. **Attack now**: the attacking move works. **Not yet**: it fails, but the position is level, so there is time to bring the missing piece. **No**: it fails and the opponent's own threat is already faster. These labels are a **rule of thumb** for deciding. What makes a verdict true in the items is the engine check behind it.

title: Hold the line in your head: six plies, nothing moved

steps.text: **Calculating without moving pieces:** play the line in your head and look at the board only at the end. You need no photographic memory, only the list from the tracing lesson, kept current: *what moved, what is gone, what is attacked now.* Moving pieces while you think is a different skill; it hides whether you can hold the position. Six plies is a first target, a rule of thumb.

steps.caption: White to move. Six plies, nothing moved. After each ply update the list: moved, gone, attacked now.

line.say: Nxg6+: the knight takes the g6 pawn, with check. Moved: knight to g6. Gone: the black g-pawn.
hxg6: the h-pawn takes the knight. Gone: the White knight. A black pawn now stands on g6.
Qxe5: queen takes queen. Gone: the black queen. The pawn on f6 now attacks the White queen.
fxe5: the f-pawn takes the queen. Gone: the White queen. A black pawn now stands on e5.
Rxf7: rook takes rook. Gone: Black's f7 rook. The rook on f8 attacks the new rook on f7.
Rxf7: rook takes rook. The rooks on f1 and f7 now face each other, and neither has a defender.

After three moves a black pawn stands on f6.

After five moves a White rook stands on f7.
After five moves the rook on f8 attacks f7.
After the six moves the White pieces that are loose are exactly: f1.
After the six moves the Black pieces that are loose are exactly: f7.

steps.text: **Where it breaks.** Captures make the list easy to update. The first *quiet* move is where lines slip: nothing leaves the board, so the old picture silently stays in your head. Rule of thumb: after every quiet move, rebuild the whole list. Holding two branches at once comes later. And when one move shows the answer, just look at the board; the effort is wasted there.

title: Where the depth goes: sort the candidates before you calculate

steps.text: Depth is a budget you split between lines, not one number for the whole position. Sort the candidates first. **Deep look:** a forcing line (checks, captures, threats) with few replies, and it keeps going. **Short look:** a move whose piece can be taken for nothing (it is loose), or a quiet move that starts nothing. **No calculation:** only one legal move. A rule of thumb, not a tested method.

steps.caption: White to move. Candidates: A) Re8+  B) Qxg7+  C) Qe7. A gets the deep look: follow it to the end.

line.say: Re8+ is check, and the rook can be taken.

Black blocks with the knight.
Qxf8 is checkmate.

claims.statement: Re8+ is legal.
Re8+ forces checkmate in 3 or fewer against the engine's best defence (depth 16).

steps.caption: Same position. B) Qxg7+ gets a short look: follow it for two plies.

line.say: Qxg7+ takes a pawn, with check. But the queen on g7 is loose: nothing defends it.
Kxg7: the king takes the queen. White has given up a queen for a pawn.

claims.statement: After Qxg7+ the White pieces that are loose are exactly: e1, g7.
Qxg7+ is at least 4 pawns worse than the best move (depth 16).
After Qxg7+ the mover's net material change along the engine's best defence is at most -2 (depth 16).

steps.text: **When the sort fails.** It uses only what you can see: checks, captures, threats, and whether the moved piece can be taken free. A quiet move can hide the best line, so give quiet candidates a short look, not a pass. In an opening line you know, recall replaces calculation. Rule of thumb: stop deepening when the position is quiet or the result is forced, not when you are tired.

title: The analysis tree: fill each cell once
outcomes: Lays out a table of candidates, replies and one-word verdicts for a forcing position
Judges a candidate by its worst cell, not its best

steps.text: A **tree** is a table you fill once. Rows are your candidates. For each, write the opponent's best replies (two is a start) and follow every branch about four plies to its end. At the end write **one word**: *mates, wins, even* or *loses* (judge by material). Fill each cell once, in order, and do not jump back. A candidate is only as good as its worst cell for you.

steps.caption: White to move. Three candidates, each followed against the best defence. A) Rh1+ : every reply loses to mate, so its cell says mates. B) Nxf7+ : White ends at least two points down, so loses. C) Rg4 : no net material change, so even. The best row is A.

line.say: Rh1+ gives check, and the king on h8 has no legal move of its own.
Black can only interpose the rook on h6.
Rxh6 is checkmate: the g3 rook covers g7 and g8, the h6 rook covers h7.

claims.statement: Rh1+ forces checkmate within two moves, whatever Black replies (depth 16).
After Rh1+ the king on h8 has no legal move.
The rook on g3 attacks g7 and g8.
After Rxh6 the rook on h6 attacks h7.
After Nxf7+ and Black's best defence White ends at least 2 points down.
Nxf7+ is at least 3 pawns worse than the best move (depth 16).
After Rg4 and the best defence White's net material change is zero.
Rg4 is at least a pawn worse than the best move (depth 16).

steps.text: **Next: a longer exercise.** This one asks you to enter a whole line, five plies, instead of a verdict word. Fill your table on paper first. A miss here is information, not failure.

**When a tree works.** It works when branches end in a clear verdict within about four plies: checks, captures, threats. It fails in two ways. A reply you never listed (the table looks complete and is not), and going back over a branch you already judged. In a quiet position few branches reach a verdict; a tree finds little. Four plies and two replies are rules of thumb.

title: Track the line: what moved, what is gone, what is attacked
outcomes: Writes what moved, what left the board and what is attacked after a two-ply line, with no piece moved
Names the loose pieces at the end of a capture and recapture, or a check and its answer
Notices when a capture removes a defender or opens a line
Runs a five-minute paper trace away from the app

steps.text: Calculating is not taking a mental photograph. It is **updating a short list** after every move: *what moved, what left the board, what is attacked now.* Start small: one candidate and one reply, so two plies, with the board in front of you and nothing moved. Then ask one question: **which piece is attacked now, and does anything defend it?**

steps.caption: Black to move. Follow the two moves without touching a piece, and update the list after each one. A piece is loose when it is attacked and nothing defends it.

line.say: Rxd2+: the d7 rook, which defended d8, leaves and takes White's rook with check.
Rxd2: White retakes. Black's rook is gone. White's d2 rook now faces the undefended d8 rook down an open file.

claims.statement: The rook on d7 defends the rook on d8.
Before the moves exactly one black piece defends d8.
After the two moves no black piece defends the rook on d8.
After the two moves one white piece attacks it.
Black's only loose piece is the rook on d8.
White has no loose piece.

steps.text: **Where tracking breaks.** A capture does two things: the capturing piece lands somewhere new, and the captured piece stops attacking and defending. A capture can also open a line behind it (a discovered attack). So ask again after every capture: *who defended what, and what is open now?* Two plies is a first size, a rule of thumb. Accuracy after the first capture matters more than length.

steps.title: Same two moves, one pawn moved
steps.prompt: In the first position the pawn stands on g6: after the rooks come off, the bishop on f5 still has a defender, so nothing is loose. In the second, the pawn is back on g7. Same two moves, one change. Predict, then check.
Tracking covers routes too. On paper, write every square a knight lands on when it travels from a1 to h8 on an empty board, then count. Counting by eye is where an extra move hides.

After a wrong check it says how many squares are missing or extra; after two misses you can ask to see the answer. The next four are silent: no hints. Hints only on request is planned, not built yet. One smaller drill. You study a position for a few seconds, then some pieces vanish, and you tap the squares a piece can reach. It trains the same habit in a simpler form: remembering what stands where, including the pieces that block a line.

**Trace card: five minutes, away from the app.** Take a position from your own game or a book diagram. Choose one candidate and the reply you expect. On paper write three lines: *moved*, *gone*, *attacked now (defended?)*. Two plies only. Then set the position up and play the two moves to check. Mark each line right or wrong. The line that fails tells you what to watch next time.

title: Counter-attack or defend: count both races
outcomes: Counts how many moves each side needs and says whether to counter-attack or defend
States the two conditions of a counter-attack: complete defence and threats that arrive first
Notices when a counter-attack that worked is one move too slow after a single change

steps.text: A **counter-attack** answers a threat with a bigger threat of your own. It works only if your own position survives the first reply and your threats arrive first. Count both races: how many moves does the opponent need, how many do you need, and are yours checks? A half-hearted mix of defending and attacking is often the weakest choice (a rule of thumb from the source idea, not a theorem).

steps.text: **It holds** when your checks or mate threats come with tempo and the opponent's king has no spare move. **It fails** when you are one move slower, or when the opponent can capture your attacker. *Rule of thumb:* if you cannot write down your whole forcing line, defend. 'The best defence is attack' is a slogan, not a theorem.

1. What is my **chief weakness**?
2. What is the opponent's **chief threat**?

title: Ahead in material, still unable to win
outcomes: Explains why an extra pawn does not win in the opposite-bishop family shown

steps.text:
A **fortress** is a set-up the stronger side cannot break, even when it is ahead. Here both sides have a bishop, on opposite colours, and White has one extra pawn, yet White cannot win.
In these examples the defender has a king beside the square the pawn needs next and a bishop with safe waiting moves. The tablebase confirms each example; it does not prove the same holds for other pawns or bishop colours.

line.say: Black waits with the bishop. The king stays where it covers b7.

claims.statement: The tablebase shows the position is a draw.
Be2 keeps the draw (tablebase).
Kd7 loses (tablebase).
The king on c8 covers b7.
White has the only pawn on the board.

steps.text:
**When it holds.** In these examples the draw holds while the black king stays next to the stop square (or on it) and the bishop has waiting moves; moving the king two files away, as in Kd7 or Kd8, loses by the tablebase.
**Rule of thumb:** Before you trust a fortress, name the square the extra pawn needs and which of your pieces guards it; then check with a tablebase or engine rather than assuming.

title: A defender's resources: meet the chief threat, nothing more
outcomes: Names the chief threat before choosing a defensive move
Lists the defender's resources and picks the one that meets that threat
Notices when a resource that worked before no longer works after one change
Does not defend when nothing is threatened

steps.text: A defender has several resources: move the piece, defend it, block, capture the attacker, make a bigger threat, vacate a weak square before supporting it, give material back. 'Five ways to meet an attack' teaches the first five. The skill here is the order: **name the chief threat first**, then choose the resource that meets it, and nothing more.

steps.caption: White to move. Black threatens Qxg2 mate (the rook on g8 backs the queen up). The pawn steps to g3.

line.say: The pawn steps up to g3. g2 is no longer there to capture, and the pawn shuts the g-file in front of the king. The engine rates it best.
Black continues; the immediate threat has been met.

claims.statement: If White passes, Black mates with Qxg2.
g3 is the engine's best move.
Bg5 is far worse.

steps.text:
**Vacate, then support.** *Rule of thumb:* if the piece standing on a weak square is itself the problem, move it first; supporting a square while the important piece still stands on it can leave both stuck.
**Over-defence.** If nothing is threatened, a defensive move is a lost move. Whichever resource you pick must stop the chief threat in the position as it is now.

title: Pawn cover: what a pawn push in front of your king gives away
outcomes: Names the pawns that form the cover in front of a castled king
Names the holes that a pawn push in front of the king creates
Tells a push that creates holes (g6) from one that creates none (h6) and from one on the other wing
Names the enemy pieces that can move to a new hole next move

steps.text: A castled king hides behind his **pawn cover**: the pawns in front of him, on his file and either side of it. A pawn that steps forward stops guarding the squares diagonally ahead of it. A **hole** is a square on your third to fifth rank that no pawn of yours attacks now or can attack later: an enemy piece can sit there and no pawn can chase it away.

steps.caption: Black to move. His king stands on g8 behind the pawns f7, g7 and h7.

line.say: The g-pawn steps to g6. It no longer guards f6 or h6, and no other pawn can.
The white queen lands on h6. No black pawn attacks that square, now or later.

claims.statement: Before the move the holes in Black's camp are a4, a5, b6, c5, c6, d6.
After g6 the holes in Black's camp are a4, a5, b6, c5, c6, d6, f6, h6.
After g6 the queen on e3 attacks h6.
No black pawn attacks h6 once the queen is there.

steps.text: A hole matters when an enemy piece can reach it and your pieces cannot cover it, so a push is a warning sign, a **rule of thumb**, not a ban. Some pushes create no hole, and a push on the other wing leaves the king's cover alone. Before a pawn move near your king, name the squares it stops guarding and the enemy pieces that could land there.

steps.title: g6 creates holes. Do h6 and a5?
steps.prompt: Black to move, same position. For each pawn move, predict: does it create a new hole on the f-, g- or h-file? Then check.
Which part is harder for you: seeing which squares a pawn stops guarding, or seeing which enemy piece can reach them? Name one pawn move near the king from your own games and check it on the board.

options: which squares the pawn stops guarding

title: Trade off the piece doing the damage
outcomes: Names the most dangerous attacking piece and the exchange that removes it
Checks that an exchange removes an attacker the opponent cannot easily replace
Tells an exchange that fails, and a position that needs no exchange

steps.text:
When you are under attack, one **exchange** can do more than any quiet defensive move: it takes away the attacker's most dangerous piece.
Ask two questions. Which enemy piece is doing the damage? Which of my pieces can trade for it?
The rest of the lesson is about when this works and when it does not.

steps.caption: White to move. Black's knight and queen are aimed at the white king and queen.

line.say: The knight takes the knight on f4, the piece that attacks the queen on e2.
Black recaptures with the queen. One pair of knights is off the board.
White has traded off the knight that was aimed at the king and queen.

claims.statement: Nxf4 is the engine's first choice.
If White passes, Black has a forced win of material or mate.
The knight on f4 attacks the queen on e2 and the pawn on g2.
Ignoring the knight with g3 is at least two pawns worse.

steps.text:
**What to check.** The exchange works when (1) it removes an attacker the opponent cannot easily replace. Two other things to check before you trade: it must not strip a defender from your own king, and it must not leave a piece loose.
**Rule of thumb:** fewer pieces help the defender. That holds only while the first condition does.

steps.title: Same attack, one change
steps.prompt: In each position White is to move. Predict whether the exchange on f4 answers the attack, then check.
Which part was hardest: spotting the most dangerous attacker, checking the three conditions, or noticing that no exchange was needed?

title: Defence by waiting: when it works
outcomes: Holds a good set-up instead of changing it without a reason
Recognises when the opponent has a way forward and waiting stops working
Switches plan at the right moment

steps.text:
**Defence by economy:** when the opponent has no clear way forward, do not change your set-up without a reason. Needless pawn moves, king walks and rook shuffles give him free tempi. Hold the best post you have and make him commit first.
**Rule of thumb** in the middlegame; the ending below is exact.

steps.caption: Black to move. White's pawn cannot advance safely yet.

line.say: Black waits: the rook stays on the sixth rank.
White commits the pawn.
Black changes plan.

claims.statement: Exact result from the tablebase: a draw.

steps.text: Waiting is right only while the opponent has no way forward. Ask: **can he improve his position by force? If not, keep the best set-up.** If he can, waiting is just passive, and you must change plan. In the next position only the pawn has moved.

steps.title: Same rook, the pawn one step further
steps.prompt: White has pushed the pawn to e6. Does the waiting move Rg6 still keep the draw? Predict first, then check.
What felt unclear: knowing when the opponent still has no way forward, or choosing the waiting move?

title: The pawn breakthrough: giving pawns to make a passed pawn
outcomes: Finds the breakthrough sacrifice in a three-against-three pawn skeleton when it exists
Predicts that the same skeleton is level when the other side moves or when the pawns stand one rank further back
Names the three things to check before trying it: who moves, how far the pawns are from queening, where the kings are

steps.text: A **breakthrough** gives up one or two pawns so that a pawn is left with no enemy pawn in front of it. It needs pawns facing pawns; the classic case is three against three on neighbouring files, and the middle pawn moves first. Look for it when your pawns are further advanced and the kings are far away. Watch one, then find it yourself.

steps.caption: White to move. The sacrifice b6 breaks through; one line is shown.

line.say: White offers the b-pawn. Black can take it with the a-pawn or the c-pawn.
Black takes with the a-pawn.
A second offer. The pawn on c6 attacks the pawn on b7.
Black takes the pawn on a5 instead.
White takes on b7. The pawn is one step from queening.
Black pushes his own pawn.
White queens first, with check.
Black's king steps to g7; White has a new queen.

claims.statement: The engine's best move is the sacrifice b6.
The engine rates the position as clearly winning for White (depth 24, evidence not proof).

steps.text: The breakthrough is **not a rule**. Here it works because White's pawns are further advanced, the kings are far from the pawns, and White moves first. Change one of these and the same skeleton may be level. Counting who queens first, and where the kings stand, decides. Having the same number of pawns, or more, does not guarantee it.

steps.title: The same skeleton, the other side to move
steps.prompt: In the first position White to move wins. Now it is Black's move, with every piece where it was. Predict the result.

steps.title: The same skeleton, one rank further back
steps.prompt: White to move wins in the first position. Now the whole skeleton is one rank lower on the board: White's pawns are on the 4th rank, Black's on the 6th. Predict the result.
Before each answer: which did you check first, who is to move, how far each side's pawns are from queening, or where the kings stand? Which one did you forget?

title: Fortresses: when more material cannot break through
outcomes: Names what a queen-against-rook-and-pawn fortress needs: covered entry squares, protected pieces and a safe waiting move
Predicts, for one-feature changes, whether a fortress holds or breaks
Tests a claimed fortress by looking for the break before relying on it

steps.text: A **fortress** is a set-up that the stronger side cannot break, even with extra material. The weaker side keeps its pieces protecting one another, covers the squares the enemy could enter, and keeps a harmless waiting move. For the best-known case, a wrong-coloured bishop with a rook pawn, see the lesson *The wrong bishop, and two knights that cannot mate*.

steps.caption: Black to move: king, rook and a pawn against a queen. Natural moves such as Ra5 and Rc6 lose; Rb6 holds. The tablebase says the position is a draw; one line is shown.

line.say: Black's rook moves to b6.
The queen checks from f8.
The king steps to a7.
The queen moves to f1.
The rook goes to d6.
The queen checks on the a-file.

claims.statement: With Black to move, the result is a draw.

steps.text: **Ask three questions.** (1) Is every square the queen could enter, or check from, covered? (2) Do the defenders protect each other, and is none forced to move away? (3) Is there a waiting move that breaks nothing? Rule of thumb: the set-up fails if some defender is attacked more often than it is protected, or if the stronger side can force a defender off its post so that an entry square is uncovered.

steps.title: One square less
steps.prompt: Black has a king, a rook and an f-pawn against a queen. In the second position the black king stands on e8 instead of f8. In the third only the white king has moved. Predict each result, then check.
Which of the three questions did you ask first? In a position where the stronger side won, which question would have shown you the break?

title: Key squares: where the king must get to
outcomes: Marks the key squares of a pawn on its 3rd or 4th rank and steps the king onto one
Predicts that a king on a key square wins whoever is to move, and that one step short the move decides
Names where the rule does not decide: an edge-file pawn with the defender near the corner, and positions with extra pieces

steps.text: A **key square** is a square where your king wins whoever is to move, provided the enemy king cannot take the pawn at once. For a pawn on its 3rd or 4th rank they are the three squares two ranks ahead, on its file and the files beside it: d6, e6 and f6 for a pawn on e4. Reach one and the pawn queens.

steps.caption: White to move. The key squares of the e4 pawn are d6, e6 and f6.

line.say: White's king steps onto d6, a key square of the pawn on e4.
Black's king goes to e8, in front of the pawn's file.
The pawn advances, with the king beside it and ahead.
Black's king goes to d8.
The pawn steps forward, protected by the king.
Black's king goes back to e8.
The pawn on e7 is protected by the king on d6.
Black's king attacks the pawn.
The king steps to d7 and protects the pawn again.
Black's king goes to f6.
The pawn queens.

claims.statement: White wins from the start position.
Kd6 wins.
Ke6 wins.
Kc6 does not win: c6 is not a key square of the e4 pawn.

steps.text: Where the key-square rule stops. One step short of a key square it says nothing, and who moves decides. For an edge-file pawn it does not apply: a defender near the corner holds. With other pieces on the board, key squares may not decide. Tested here only on the squares in this lesson; the general rule is standard theory.

steps.title: The king on a key square, or one step short
steps.prompt: With White's king on the key square d6 and Black to move, White wins. Now put White's king one step back, on d5, with Black still to move. Predict the result.
Before each answer: did you find the squares two ranks in front of the pawn first? And when the king was one step short, did you check who was to move?

title: The king as a fighter: pawn endings the active king decides
outcomes: Chooses a king move over a pawn move when the king can reach the enemy pawns first
Counts the two kings' distances to the pawns that matter and predicts win or draw
Sees that one step of king activity, for either side, can flip the result

steps.text: In the ending the king stops being a target and becomes a **fighting piece**. A king that reaches the enemy pawns first can win what pawn moves cannot. The question to ask is a count: how many king steps does each side need to reach the pawns that matter? Look at the kings, not at the pawns.

steps.caption: White to move wins, but only with Ke6. One line is shown.

line.say: The king goes forward, not a pawn.
Black's king comes back.
White's king steps to f7, next to the pawns.
Black pushes a pawn.
White pushes a pawn.
Black's king keeps coming.
White's king attacks the pawn on g5.
Black's king is still a step too far.

claims.statement: White wins from the start position.

steps.text: **It is a race, so one step matters.** King activity wins when your king reaches the enemy pawns before the other king can defend them. If your king is one step slower, or the defender's king one step nearer, a win can become a draw. Predict what changes in the look-alikes.

steps.title: One step less active
steps.prompt: White's king on e4 wins. What if it is on e3, one rank back? Predict, then check.

steps.title: One step nearer for Black
steps.prompt: Ke5 against Kc8 wins with the right king move. What if Black's king is on d8? Predict, then check.
Before you answered: did you count the two kings' steps to the pawns, or did you look at the pawn moves first? Which gave you the right answer more often?

title: Knight endings: count the journey
outcomes: Counts a knight's route between two squares (four moves from a1 to b2) and says whose knight arrives first
Compares a knight's count with the two moves a rim pawn needs to queen, and checks the guess against the tablebase
Predicts how one change (the extra pawn's file, the knight's square, Black's king, a bishop instead of a knight) can flip a knight ending

steps.text: Knights are slow. A knight needs up to six moves to cross the board, and every move changes the colour of its square. So in knight endings you **count the journey**: the number of knight moves, not the number of squares. First see the colour change on the board, then count a route yourself.

steps.caption: White to move. The knight on d4 stands on a dark square and has eight moves. Every one of them lands on a light square.

line.say: The knight goes from a dark square, d4, to a light square, e6.
Black's king makes a waiting move.
Another knight move, another change of colour: c5 is dark.
Black waits again.
Light again. After an even number of knight moves the knight is back on a dark square.

claims.statement: The knight on d4 has exactly these eight moves.

steps.text: **Counting judges a race.** Black's pawn on a3 needs two moves to queen. A knight that reaches b3 or c2, the squares that cover a1, in two moves is in the race. But counting is only a *rule of thumb*: a check gains a move, and the kings matter too. Check the result with a **tablebase** (exact results for positions with few pieces).

steps.title: Can the knight stop the rim pawn?
steps.prompt: In the first position the knight stands on f3. In the second it stands on g3; in the third White's king is on g8, not h8. Predict both, then check.

steps.text: *Rule of thumb:* a passed pawn far from the other pawns (an **outside passed pawn**) ties down the defender's king and knight, so it often wins. Move the same pawn closer and the ending can be a draw. Predict, then check.

steps.title: An outside passed pawn
steps.prompt: In the first position White's a-pawn is passed and far from the kingside. In the second the extra pawn stands on h4 instead of a4; in the third White's knight is on d3, not c3. Predict both, then check.
Which part is least clear: counting a knight's route, comparing it with the pawn's moves, or remembering that the kings count too?

title: King and pawn against king: the king leads
outcomes: Wins king and pawn against king by bringing the king in front of the pawn first and pushing the pawn only when a push is needed
Holds the draw as the defender by standing in front of the pawn and taking the opposition
Recognises when the plan fails: the defender facing the king with the move against it, a rook pawn with the defender near the corner

steps.text: **King and pawn against king** is decided by the kings more than by the pawn. Attacker: bring your king in front of the pawn and push only when a push is needed (a **rule of thumb**, not a law). Defender: stand in front of the pawn and keep the opposition. Pushing early is the classic way to throw a win away. Watch one win, then test the rule.

steps.caption: White to move. Each of the king moves Kf5, Kd4 and Kf4 wins; the push f4 only draws.

line.say: The king goes first. Kd4 and Kf4 also win here; the push f4 only draws.
Black's king goes to e7.
White's king keeps going, further ahead of the pawn.
Black's king steps to f8.
Only now does the pawn move, one square, with the king well ahead of it.
Black's king steps along the back rank.
White's king advances again.
Black's king goes to e7.
The pawn follows the king.
Black's king goes to d6.
The pawn steps forward again, protected by the king on g7.
Black's king cannot reach the pawn.
One step from queening, and the king guards the queening square.

claims.statement: White wins from the start position.
Kf5 wins.
Kd4 wins.
Kf4 wins.
The push f4 only draws.

steps.text: The plan is a **rule of thumb**; it fails in two ways. The enemy king may cover the squares ahead, so a pawn push is the only winning move. Or nothing wins: the defender faces your king and you are to move, or the pawn is on the edge file with his king near the corner. Ask: can my king get ahead of the pawn, and who is to move?

title: Lucena and Philidor: the two rook endings to know
outcomes: Explains in plain words how the attacker wins with a pawn on the seventh (Lucena) and how the defender draws with the rook on the sixth rank (Philidor)
Avoids two tempting errors in the Lucena position: promoting at once and blocking a check with a loose rook
Knows the Philidor check from behind needs a rook placement that White's rook cannot punish

steps.text: Two rook endings to know. In **Lucena** the pawn stands on the seventh, your king is in front of it and the enemy king is cut off; you win by getting the king out of the way of checks. In **Philidor** the defender keeps the rook on the sixth rank and checks from behind once the pawn advances. Both are plans with conditions.

steps.caption: Lucena-type: White to move wins. One winning line is shown.

line.say: A rook check pushes Black's king away.
Black's king steps to h7.
The rook goes to the fourth rank.
Black's king steps to h6.
White's king steps out of the queening square.
Black's rook checks along the f-file.
The king steps off the file.
Black's rook checks again, now along the e-file.

claims.statement: White wins from the start position.

steps.text: **Conditions.** Lucena needs a pawn on the seventh, your king in front and the enemy king cut off. Promoting at once, or blocking a check with a loose rook, throws the win away. **Philidor** is a plan: a rook on the sixth rank is a good default, not the only drawing idea. Its check from behind fails if White's rook can capture it.

steps.title: Same Philidor move, rook one rank apart
steps.prompt: White's pawn is on e6. Black plays Ra1. Does it hold if White's rook is on h2? On h1? Predict, then check.
In which position did you want to promote or to check at once? What did you not look at before you moved: the rook's safety, or what the other rook could take?

title: Mating a lone king: queen, rook, and the stalemate trap
outcomes: Mates a bare king with queen or rook and king without stalemating it
Recognises checkmate, stalemate and neither at a glance
Checks, before every non-mating move, that the lone king still has a legal move and that the piece is safe

steps.text: To mate a bare king, a queen or rook alone is not enough: push the king to an edge and bring your own king close. Before every move that is not mate, ask one question: **can Black still make a legal move?** If Black has no legal move and is not in check, the game is a draw, however much material you have.

steps.caption: White to move: mate in three. The checks Qg5+ and Qh5+ only draw.

line.say: A quiet queen move, a knight's move from the king, with no check.
Black's king steps to h5.
Another quiet queen move. The white king stays on f3.
Black's king steps to h4.
The white king guards g4, so the queen mates.

steps.text: **Three checks before every move.** 1. If it is not mate, can Black's king still move? 2. Can the king capture your piece for free? 3. Is your own king close enough to protect the final check? A move that takes the last square without giving check is stalemate. Now one look-alike: the same queen move, one king step apart.

steps.title: Same queen move, one king step apart
steps.prompt: White plays Qg6 in both. Black's king is on h7 or on h8. Predict the result each time, then check.
Which of your checks (Black's legal moves, the safety of your piece, your king's distance) did you skip before a move? What will you check first next time?

title: Two bishops against a lone king
outcomes: Mates with two bishops and the king against a bare king from a position given, finding the quiet first move
Avoids the stalemate by counting the lone king's legal moves before a quiet move
Tells two bishops on opposite colours (can mate) from two on one colour (cannot)

steps.text: Two bishops on **opposite-coloured squares** can mate a lone king, but only with their own king close by. Your king takes away flight squares, the bishops attack squares of both colours near the corner, and a quiet bishop move (a waiting move) or a check forces the last steps. Watch one finish, then find the first move yourself.

steps.caption: White to move mates in three. Black's king is in the corner a8; White's king covers b7 and b8.

line.say: A quiet move. The bishop now covers a6, so after Ka7 and Bd4+ the king cannot step to a6.
Black's king steps to a7.
The dark bishop checks along the diagonal to a7.
Black's king goes back to a8.
The light bishop checks on the long diagonal. Mate: the king covers b7 and b8, the other bishop a7.

claims.statement: Be2 starts a forced mate in three.
Black's king has the single legal move Ka7 after Be2, as it did before: Be2 does not take a flight square away.
After Be2 the bishop attacks a6.
Before Be2 the black king already has exactly one legal move.

steps.text: Three conditions. The bishops must stand on **opposite colours**: in the example two bishops on one colour only draw. Your king must come close; bishops alone do not mate. And count Black's moves before any quiet move: if the king has no legal move and is not in check, the game is **stalemate**, a draw.

steps.title: Opposite colours or the same colour
steps.prompt: In the first position White wins. Now one bishop stands on a square of the other colour. Predict the result.

steps.title: The right check, or the stalemate
steps.prompt: In the first position Bb7+ mates in two. Now White plays the other bishop move instead. Is that checkmate, stalemate or neither?
Before each move or answer: did you count the lone king's legal moves, and did you check the colour of both bishops? Which did you forget?

title: Bishop and knight against a lone king: the right corner
outcomes: States the two phases and the textbook corner rule
Finds the first move of a bishop-and-knight mate with the king already near the right corner

steps.text: **Bishop and knight** can mate a bare king, but by the textbook rule only around a corner of the **bishop's colour**: with a light-squared bishop, h1 or a8. There are two phases. outcomes: Classifies a queen against a pawn one step from queening as win or draw from the pawn's file, when the stronger king is far away

steps.text: A queen usually beats a lone pawn. But when the pawn is one step from queening and its own king stands beside it, a **stalemate** trap can save it: a careless queen move leaves the weaker side with no legal move. The pawn's **file** decides whether the trap exists. Watch one trap first, then compare files.

steps.caption: White to move: a queen against a pawn on a2, the black king in the corner and the white king far away. The tablebase says this position is a draw. One tempting move is shown.

steps.text: **When the draw works.** In this course's set-ups (stronger king far away, weaker king beside the pawn), a pawn on the seventh rank draws on the a-, c-, f- and h-files (rook and bishop pawns) and loses on the b-, d-, e- and g-files. title: Rook endings: four habits and where they fail
outcomes: Puts the rook behind a passed pawn and predicts how the result changes when the rook stands in front of it
Checks which side of the rook's file the enemy king stands on, and predicts how the result changes when the king is not cut off
Predicts win or draw with the rook on the seventh rank, and names a position where the seventh rank is not enough

steps.text:
Four rook-ending habits.
**Behind:** put the rook behind a passed pawn.
**Cut off:** keep the enemy king away along a file or rank.
**Seventh:** a rook on the seventh rank can shut the enemy king on the back rank.
**Distance:** the defender's rook checks from far away.
Each is a *rule of thumb* with exceptions. A **tablebase** (exact results for few pieces) checks every position.

steps.caption: White to move wins. The rook stands on e4, behind the passed pawn on e5. One line is shown.

line.say: The pawn advances. The rook on e4 defends it from behind along the open file.
Black's rook runs to the far end of the board.
The pawn reaches e7. The rook still defends it from behind, across more squares.
Black's rook takes the square in front of the pawn.
White's king steps up the board towards the pawn.

claims.statement: White wins from the start position.
1.e6 keeps the win.
The pawn on e5 is passed.
White's rook is on e4.
After e6 the rook defends the pawn.
After e7 the rook still defends the pawn.

steps.text: **Why behind?** From behind, the rook defends the pawn along the file after every push, and each push gives the rook more open squares behind the pawn. In front of the pawn it blocks the pawn's path and loses a square with each push. This is a *rule of thumb*: some positions need a passive rook instead. First test the habit: predict each position, then check.

steps.title: Behind or in front?
steps.prompt: In the first position White's rook is behind its passed pawn. In the second it stands on g7, in front of the pawn; in the third Black's rook is on c6. Predict both, then check.

steps.text: **Cut off, and when it fails.** A rook on a file keeps the enemy king on the far side of that file, away from your pawn. If the king is already on the pawn's side of the file, there is nothing to cut off, and the win can vanish. A *rule of thumb*: check which side of the rook's file the king stands on, then predict.

steps.title: Is the king cut off?
steps.prompt: In the first position White's rook on e1 keeps Black's king on the far side of the e-file from the pawn. In the second the king stands on c7, on the pawn's side; in the third Black's rook is on b8, not a8. Predict both, then check.

steps.text:
**Seventh rank:** a rook there attacks the whole rank if it is open, keeping the enemy king on the back rank. It is strongest with an advanced passed pawn, but no guarantee.
**Distance:** the defender's rook checks from far away, where the king cannot attack it. A check right next to the king can simply lose the rook.
Both are *rules of thumb*. Predict, then check.

title: The tablebase lab: test a claim, do not just quote it
outcomes: States what a tablebase result is (exact for the side to move, seven pieces or fewer) and what it does not say
Decides whether a position can be looked up at all
Tests a conjecture with a position where it should hold and one where it should fail, predicting each result first

steps.text:
A **tablebase** stores every position with few pieces (seven or fewer, kings included) and its exact result under the usual rules for the side to move: win, draw or loss with best play. It is not an engine's opinion.
It gives the result, not the reason. This app has no tablebase tool, so the lab here is a paper-and-browser routine using any online tablebase.

The lab routine:
**1.** Write the conjecture as one sentence, with its conditions.
**2.** Write two positions that differ by one feature: one where it should hold, one where it should fail.
**3.** Predict both results before you look.
**4.** Query the tablebase.
**5.** Record the result and a reason a person could check by hand.
One failure refutes a conjecture. Many successes do not prove it.

steps.title: When can the lab answer?
steps.prompt: A seven-piece rook ending, the same ending with one more pawn, and an opening position. For each, decide whether a tablebase can answer, then check.

steps.text:
Conditions. A tablebase answers only for seven pieces or fewer. It names a result and never a reason, so 'win' needs your own checkable explanation before you teach it to anyone.
Rule of thumb: if you cannot state a reason another person could check, you hold a fact, not an understanding.

steps.prompt: Run steps 1 to 3 of the lab now on a claim from a book, a video or your own games (seven pieces or fewer). Save the note, then do the lookup later in any online tablebase and write the result and a reason beside it on paper; the app cannot reopen a saved note.

steps.text:
A queen is stronger than a rook, but it does not win by size alone. It wins by **forcing**: a check makes the king move, then one queen move attacks the king and the rook together (a fork), or the rook behind the king on the same line (a skewer).
In the positions below the rook falls. Your job: find the check that separates the rook from its king.

line.say: Qa1+ is check along the first rank. Black must answer it.

Now the queen takes the rook.

steps.text: A **tablebase** is a stored list of exact results for positions with few pieces. It gives the result with best play by both sides: win, draw or loss. It does not say how many moves a person needs, or how hard the defence is to find; that is not measured here. Read 'the queen wins' as a statement about perfect play, then practise the method until it is routine.

Check three things before a check.
**1. Who moves?** The rook's side to move may fork king and queen and draw.
**2. Stalemate.** Taking the rook can leave a lone king with no legal move: a draw.
**3. Pawns.** An advanced pawn can change the result; this method is for queen against rook alone.
Before each check, ask: can the rook then check and hit the queen?

steps.text: Sometimes the winning position is on the board, but the wrong player is to move. A king can pass the move. Stepping out and back takes **two** moves, and the opponent can answer with a two-move shuffle. Walking round a triangle of three squares takes **three**. That is **triangulation**: your king ends where it started and the opponent has to move.

Step three: White's king is back on a6. The placement is the starting one, but now Black must move.

steps.text: **When it works.** The three squares must be free and safe, and the defender must have no triangle or waiting move of his own. If he has one, he answers in kind and the draw is back. Rule of thumb: ask first whether the position would win with the opponent to move; if it would and you are to move, look for a triangle. Opposition stays the first tool.

title: Zugzwang: when having the move is a burden
outcomes: Recognises a reciprocal zugzwang in a blocked king-and-pawn ending: whoever must move loses

steps.text: **Zugzwang** means every move you have makes your position worse; you would rather pass. In some blocked pawn endings both sides are in zugzwang, so whoever has to move loses. Then the fight is about the move itself: the winner tries to reach that position with the other side to move.

steps.caption: White to move. All five White moves lose; one line is shown.

Black's king takes the pawn on e4.

White's king keeps following.
Black's pawn is free to run.
White's king heads for the corner.
Black's king keeps close to the pawn.

claims.statement: With White to move, White loses.

steps.text: **Conditions.** Mutual zugzwang needs blocked pawns and no spare moves: only the kings can move. Then the side to move loses. It is a heuristic about such positions, not a law: when a king stands one step away, or has a detour that loses a move (**triangulation**), the move can be won back. Predict what changes.

title: Which squares does a piece attack?
outcomes: Taps every square a rook, bishop, knight or pawn attacks when other pieces stand in the way
Stops a line at the first piece it meets and keeps the squares behind it out
Knows a pawn attacks diagonally ahead, even when blocked, and not straight ahead
Says a defended piece is still attacked

steps.text:
A piece **attacks** a square when it could capture an enemy piece standing there (a pinned piece is covered in the check card below). If the square holds a piece of its own side, we say the piece **defends** it.
An attacked square need not hold anything yet. And the squares a piece attacks are not always the squares it moves to.

steps.caption: White to move. The lit squares are the squares the rook on e3 attacks.

line.say: The rook can take the pawn on e7. It is the first piece on the file; e8 behind it was never attacked.

claims.statement: These twelve squares are exactly the rook's attacked squares.
A black pawn stands on e7.
The rook can capture the pawn on e7.

steps.text:
Check before you trust 'attacks'.
**Lines:** a rook, bishop or queen attacks up to and including the first piece it meets; squares behind it are not attacked.
**Pawns:** the squares diagonally ahead (one square on an edge file), even when blocked; never straight ahead.
**Pinned pieces** still attack their squares (an enemy king may not step there), though they may be unable to capture. A defended piece is still attacked.

title: The board and its square names
outcomes: Names any square from its file and rank
Finds a named square on the board, from White's side or Black's

steps.text: A chessboard has 64 squares. The columns are called **files** and are named with the letters **a** to **h**, left to right as White sees the board. The rows are called **ranks** and are numbered **1** to **8**, starting at White's side. Every square has a name: its file letter, then its rank number. The white king starts on **e1**.

steps.caption: Watch the white pawn travel from e2 to e4. Every square keeps its name.

line.say: The pawn on e2 moves to e4.
Black's pawn on e7 moves to e5.

steps.text: To write a move down, use the piece's letter and the square it goes to: **K** king, **Q** queen, **R** rook, **B** bishop, **N** knight. Pawns have no letter, so a pawn move is just the square: **e4**. A capture adds an **x**: **Nxe5** means the knight captures on e5.

title: Taking pieces, and what pieces are worth
outcomes: Gives a rough point value to each piece and uses it to compare trades
Checks whether a capture is guarded before taking
Knows that material values are a guide, and that checkmate beats them

steps.text: You **capture** by moving onto an enemy piece and taking it off the board. Captures are never forced. To compare trades, players count **material**, giving each piece a rough value: pawn 1, knight 3, bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9. The king has no value because it cannot be captured; it is checkmated instead. These numbers are a first guide, not a law.

steps.caption: The bishop takes a knight that nothing guards. White is 3 of material ahead.

line.say: The bishop takes the knight on e5.
Black has no piece that can take the bishop back.

steps.text: Before you take, ask: **is the piece guarded?** A piece is guarded (or defended) when a friend could take back on that square. If it is guarded, compare what you give up with what you win. If you win more than you lose, the capture can still be good.

The pawn takes the knight: White loses 3.

steps.text: The material values are a guide, not the whole truth. The next position shows one way they can mislead: checkmate ends the game, whatever the material count says. Later you will meet other cases where a piece is worth more or less than its usual value.

title: Castling, and when you cannot
outcomes: Castles kingside and queenside
Knows the four conditions and which attacked squares matter
Spots when castling is not available

steps.text: **Castling** is the one move where two pieces move at once. The king goes two squares toward a rook, and that rook jumps over to the king's other side. It tucks the king away and brings a rook into the game. You can castle toward the h-file (kingside) or toward the a-file (queenside).

steps.caption: White castles kingside: the king goes to g1 and the rook to f1. Black castles queenside.

line.say: The king goes to g1 and the rook jumps to f1.
Black castles the other way: king to c8, rook to d8.

steps.text: You may castle only if: the king and that rook have never moved; every square between them is empty; the king is not in check; and the king does not pass over or land on an attacked square. The rook's own path does not have to be safe.

title: Check, checkmate and stalemate
outcomes: Gets out of check in one of the three ways, and sees when a way is impossible
Tells check, checkmate and stalemate apart
Gives mate without stalemating by accident

steps.text: When your king is attacked it is in **check**. You must fix it at once, in one of three ways: **move** the king, **block** the attack with a piece, or **capture** the piece that gives check. You may never make a move that leaves your own king in check.

steps.caption: White is in check. The king can step away, the bishop can block, or the rook can capture.

steps.text: If there is **no** way out of check, it is **checkmate**: the game ends and the player in check loses. If the player to move is **not** in check but has no legal move, it is **stalemate**: the game is a draw. The two look alike, but the results are opposite.

steps.caption: The rook checks along the back rank (the row where the pieces start). The king's own pawns block its escape. Checkmate.

title: Is this piece safe? Loose pieces and counting
outcomes: Spots loose pieces (attacked and not defended) on either side
Counts attackers and defenders of a square
Decides whether to start captures on a square by adding up the swaps, cheapest piece first

steps.text: A piece is **attacked** when an enemy piece could capture it. It is **defended** when a friendly piece could take back on that square. A piece that is attacked and **not defended** is **loose** (also called **hanging**): it can be taken for free. Spotting loose pieces, yours and theirs, is the first safety habit.

steps.caption: The queen attacks the pawn on b6 and the bishop on d5. Only one of them is loose.

steps.text: When several pieces fight over one square, count. List the attackers and the defenders. Start captures with your cheapest attacker. Add up what each side takes and gives, and stop when the next swap would lose more than it wins. More attackers than defenders is not always enough.

steps.caption: Two attackers, one defender, and the pawn goes first. Count the swaps.

title: The knight: the piece that jumps
outcomes: Taps every square a knight can jump to, including captures
Knows the knight is not blocked by pieces in between, unlike rooks and bishops

steps.text: The **knight** moves in an L: two squares along a rank or a file, then one square to the side. It is the only piece that **jumps over** other pieces. It lands on an empty square or captures an enemy piece, but never lands on its own piece. Every jump ends on a square of the opposite colour.

steps.caption: The knight jumps over the ring of pawns. Seven landing squares are open.

steps.text: Rooks, bishops and queens need a clear path. A knight does not: it only needs a landing square that is not held by its own piece. That is why, at the start of a game, a knight can move while most other pieces cannot.

steps.title: A crowd does not stop a knight
steps.prompt: Every back-rank piece is boxed in by pawns. Predict first: which of these can move at the start, the knight on b1 or the bishop on c1?

steps.caption: To reach e5 from g1 the knight needs two jumps: first f3, then e5.

line.say: First jump: from g1 to f3.
Black's king makes a move.
Second jump: from f3 to e5.

title: Checkmate in one: four patterns
outcomes: Finds a checkmate in one in the common patterns: back rank, queen next to the king, two rooks, queen with a bishop, knight
Checks every exit before calling a check checkmate
Says 'no mate' when there is none

steps.text: **Checkmate** means the king is attacked and cannot escape: there is no safe square, nothing that can capture the attacker, and no way to block it. A **mate in one** does all of that with one move. A few shapes appear again and again. The first is the **back-rank mate**.

steps.caption: The rook checks along the back rank. The king's own pawns block its escape.

line.say: The rook slides to the eighth rank. It is checkmate.

steps.text: Before you call a check mate, check every exit: can the king step anywhere, can the checking piece be captured, can the check be blocked? A back-rank mate needs the king's own pawns to stand in front of it, with no square for the king to run to.

steps.title: Same rook, one pawn moved
steps.prompt: Black's h-pawn stands on h6 instead of h7. Predict first: is there still a mate in one?

steps.caption: After Ra8+ the king simply steps to h7. A pawn move gave it a square to run to.

line.say: The king escapes to h7. It was check, not checkmate.

steps.text: Three more shapes. A **queen next to the king** is safe when your own king or another piece protects her. **Two rooks** can take turns: one holds a rank, the other gives check. A **knight's check** cannot be blocked, so it mates a king that has no square.

title: Reading and writing a move
outcomes: Names the piece, the squares and any capture, check or castling in a written move
Plays an eight-move score on the board, from either colour and on a turned board
Adds a file letter (or a rank number when both pieces share a file) when two pieces of the same kind can make the move
Knows that marks such as ! and ? do not change the move

steps.text: A move record says **which piece** and **where it lands**. K king, Q queen, R rook, B bishop, N knight; a pawn move has no letter. **x** capture, **+** check, **#** checkmate, **O-O** castling kingside (**O-O-O** queenside), **=Q** a pawn becomes a queen. A number counts one White move and Black's reply: 1.e4 d5. Dots (1...d5) mark Black's move when a score starts with it.

steps.caption: A short score, played from the start. Read each record, then watch the move.

line.say: 1.e4: no letter, so a pawn moves, to e4.
1...d5: three dots mark a Black move shown alone. In a row it is written 1.e4 d5.
2.exd5: the e-pawn captures on d5. The x marks a capture.
2...Qxd5: the queen (Q) captures the pawn on d5.
3.Nc3: N is the knight; it lands on c3.
3...Qa5: no x, because nothing is captured on a5.
4.d4: a pawn move again, so there is no letter.
4...Nf6: Black's knight goes to f6.

claims.statement: 1.e4 is legal from the start.
A white pawn stands on e2 at the start.

steps.text: A record must name exactly one move. If two pieces of the same kind can reach the square, add the file the mover leaves from (**Nbd2**); if both stand on the same file, add the rank instead (**R1a3**). The marks **!** and **?** are a writer's opinion; they change nothing. The same record works for either colour and for a board turned around: square names do not change.

title: Your first moves: three habits
outcomes: Takes space in the centre with a pawn on move one

steps.text: Early in a game your pieces start behind pawns. Three habits help: **1.** Put a pawn in the centre (e4 or d4) to give pieces room. **2.** Bring your knights and bishops out toward the middle, each piece once. **3.** Castle early to tuck your king away. They are habits, not laws: a threat from your opponent comes first.

steps.text: Pieces work best where they reach many squares. A knight in the middle of the board reaches up to eight squares; on the edge, at most four, and in a corner only two. So bring pieces toward the centre, and bring each new piece out rather than moving the same one again and again.

title: The pawn: moves and captures are different
outcomes: Taps every square a pawn can move to, including the two-square start and diagonal captures
Knows a pawn cannot capture straight ahead and is blocked by any piece in front of it

steps.text: **Pawns** move straight forward, one square at a time, and never backward. From their starting square they may move two squares if both are empty. But pawns **capture** differently: one square diagonally forward. A pawn cannot capture straight ahead, and any piece directly in front of it blocks it.

steps.caption: Forward to e3 or e4, or a capture on d3. The pawn goes diagonally only to capture.

steps.text: Two details cause most pawn mistakes. The two-square jump is only for a pawn's first move, and only if both squares are empty. And a pawn captures diagonally, never straight ahead. Before moving a pawn ask: has it moved yet? And is the square ahead empty?

title: The queen and the king
outcomes: Taps every square a queen can reach
Knows the king may never step onto an attacked square or next to the enemy king
Tells which of the pieces on the board can reach or capture on a square

steps.text: The **queen** is the strongest piece. She moves like a rook and a bishop combined: any distance along a rank, a file or a diagonal. She cannot jump, and she captures the same way: by landing on an enemy piece.

steps.caption: Eight directions. Two white pawns and two black pawns decide where each line stops.

steps.text: The **king** moves one square in any direction. He is the piece you must never lose, so there is one extra rule: **a king may never move onto a square the enemy attacks** (a square where an enemy piece could capture). That also means two kings can never stand on neighbouring squares.

steps.caption: The black rook attacks the whole fifth rank. The king cannot step onto it.

steps.text: The king can capture too, but only if the piece is not guarded. A piece is **guarded** (or defended) when a friendly piece could recapture on its square. Ask before you capture: which enemy pieces attack the square I am about to land on?

title: The rook and the bishop
outcomes: Taps every square a rook or bishop can reach, including captures and blocked lines

steps.text: The **rook** moves in straight lines: along a rank (sideways) or a file (up and down), as far as it likes. It cannot jump over pieces. To **capture**, it lands on an enemy piece and takes it off the board. It can never land on a square holding its own piece.

steps.caption: The rook slides until something is in the way. It can take the black pawn on d7, but not go past it.

steps.text: The **bishop** moves in diagonals, as far as it likes, and cannot jump. A bishop stays on one colour of square for the whole game: one bishop travels on light squares, the other on dark squares. Captures work just like the rook's.

steps.caption: Four diagonals, but the white pawn on b2 shortens one of them.

steps.text: Before you move a rook or bishop to a square, ask three questions. Is the square on one of my piece's lines? Is anything standing between? Whose piece, if any, is on the square? Empty or enemy: allowed. Your own piece: not allowed.

title: En passant, promotion and draws
outcomes: Captures en passant, and knows it must be done at once

steps.text: **En passant** means 'in passing'. When an enemy pawn jumps two squares and lands right beside your pawn, you may capture it as if it had moved only one square. You must do it on the very next move, or the chance is gone.

steps.caption: Black's pawn jumped from d7 to d5. White captures it as if it had stopped on d6.

steps.text: A pawn that reaches the last rank is **promoted**: you choose a queen, rook, bishop or knight. It can promote by moving straight ahead or by capturing diagonally. Before you push, check the promotion square. If an enemy piece attacks it, the new piece can be captured at once.

A game is a **draw** when: a player has no legal move and is not in check (stalemate); the same position occurs three times (repetition); fifty moves pass without a capture or a pawn move; there are not enough pieces to checkmate; or both players agree. Do not assume that an extra piece always wins.

title: Before every move: two questions
outcomes: Names what the opponent's last move threatens, including a checkmate threat

steps.text: Before every move, ask two questions. **1. What does my opponent's last move threaten?** (a capture, a check, a checkmate). **2. Is any of my pieces loose?** (attacked, and not defended). Only then choose your own move. Strong players do this all the time; beginners lose most games by skipping it.

steps.text: The second question looks at your own side. After each opponent move, scan your pieces: is any of them attacked and not defended? If nothing is loose and nothing is threatened, you are free to follow your opening habits.

Now play your first games. Play simply: take the centre, bring your pieces out, castle, and ask the two questions before every move. Do not worry about winning. The goal is to notice. After a game, mark **one moment where you were unsure** and what you expected your opponent to do.

**A mistake has a cause, and the cause decides what to practise.** Five boxes:

**Seen but miscalculated:** you looked and the count was wrong.

**Out of book:** the position or plan was new to you.

**When it holds.** The compensation is real if what you gave buys something that outlasts the opponent's next few moves. **It fails** when lines are closed, when the opponent has already developed, or when the engine rates you more than half a pawn behind.
**Rule of thumb:** give material back only for something tangible. The engine verdict is evidence at one depth, not proof.

steps.text:
In this course a **threat** is a move that would win material or mate if the other side did nothing. The **initiative** belongs to the side whose moves carry threats the opponent must answer, while the opponent has none.
To find it, list the threats for both sides. The side to move does not automatically have it.

steps.text:

**Rule of thumb:** not every move needs a threat. When neither side has any threat, as in the drawn rook ending below, nobody has the initiative.

steps.text:
A **held threat** is a capture or attack you could carry out but have not. While it hangs there, the opponent's pieces are tied to answering it. Carrying it out frees them.
So ask before every capture: do I gain something at once, or can I add pressure first? This lesson names the threat and the piece it ties down.

steps.text:
**When to hold, when to cash in.** Hold when the capture only trades and a quiet move adds an attacker. Cash in when the capture gains material at once.
**Rule of thumb:** execute a threat only if something is gained immediately. A held threat is worth nothing if the target can simply move or be defended.

steps.text:
The **safety scan** is the two questions from the threat lesson, run on every move in about ten seconds.
**1. What did my opponent's last move threaten or open?**
**2. Is any of my pieces loose, or attacked by something cheaper?**
This is a habit to try, not a law. It catches obvious dangers, not deep ones.

**Defended is not the same as safe.** A defended piece that a *cheaper* piece attacks can still be lost: the cheaper piece takes, you retake, and you gave up more than you won.
Ask: **is it attacked, and what would the trade cost me?**

title: Candidates and short lines

steps.text: Do not play the first good-looking move. Make a short **candidate list**: two to four moves, forcing moves first. Then follow each for about three **plies** (a ply is one move by one side): your move, the opponent's best reply, your next move. Drop candidates that clearly fail. Two to four is a habit to try, not a rule.

steps.text: To follow a line you must hold the board in your head. **Drill:** you study a position for 15 seconds, then some pieces vanish from the board. You must still say where a piece can go. This is a training exercise for seeing lines, not a chess rule.

**Short lines have limits.** Three plies are enough when every move is forcing. They can mislead when a sacrifice pays off later: a line that looks bad at ply three can be mate at ply five. And in quiet positions the candidates may not separate at all.
Ask: **is the last move of my line quiet or forcing?**

title: How deep? Spend calculation where it pays

steps.text:
Depth is a **budget**, not a virtue. Habits to try:
**Go deep** when every move in the line is a check, capture or threat: the replies are few.
**Stop** when the position is quiet and you can compare it, when you have found a refutation, or when the clock says so.
**Spend more** at critical moments, less at routine ones.

steps.text:
**Four stop signs:** the position is quiet; you found a refutation; no line changes the material (the moment is routine); time. And **two warning signs** that you stopped too early: your line ends on a capture, or on a check.
Depth allocation is a habit to try; nobody has measured the best split.

title: Cross out, then check from the other side
outcomes: Crosses out candidates one at a time with one concrete reply each
Checks the surviving move from the opponent's seat, in a different order from the one that found it
Finds a quiet refutation that a search of captures and checks misses
Says when elimination does not apply (a single legal move) and where verification is worth its time

steps.text: Two steps, in this order. **Eliminate:** for each candidate, look for one concrete reply that refutes it: a capture, a check, a threat. Cross out what falls. **Verify:** for the survivor, change seats. In the position after your move, list the opponent's checks, captures and threats, then find his best reply. Do not re-walk your own line in the same order: it tends to repeat the same blind spot.

steps.caption: White to move. One candidate is crossed out in two moves.

line.say: Nxe8+ takes a rook with check. It looks strong.
The rook on f8 takes the knight, and nothing of White's defends it.

claims.statement: Nxe8+ is at least 300 centipawns worse than the best move (depth 16).
After Nxe8+ the knight on e8 is attacked by 2 black pieces.
After Nxe8+ the knight on e8 is loose.

steps.text: **Verifying is not recalculating.** You found the line from your side, so walking it again in the same order shows the same things. Switch sides and change the order: his checks first, then his captures, then his quiet threats. **Rule of thumb:** spend it where a mistake is costly and cannot be taken back. A position with one legal move has nothing to cross out.

**Some refutations are quiet.** A search of captures and checks crosses out the easy candidates. A candidate that survives that search may still fail to a quiet move: one that captures nothing and gives no check but makes a threat or traps a piece. That is why the survivor gets its own look from the other side. Next: find a quiet refutation.

**Test the escape squares before you trust a perpetual.** A run of checks forces a draw only if every reply Black has leads back into the same checks: no capture of the checker, no block, and no king step that gets out of them. List the king's squares first, then ask where each one leads. A free square often ends the checks, but not always.

steps.caption: White is far behind. Can the knight keep checking?

Kh7 is forced.
Nf8+. Again nothing can take it, and the king's only square is h8.
Kh8 is forced. Ng6+ would now repeat the position after the first check.

After Ng6+ no black piece attacks the knight on g6.
After Ng6+ Kh7 Nf8+ the black king on h7 has exactly one legal move.
After Nf8+ no black piece attacks the knight on f8.

steps.text: A **novelty** is a move that leaves known play where it is at least as good as the old move, and is new to the person you play. 'Known' means known to someone: a book, a database, your opponent. Two tests: is it new where it matters, and can you say why it works? The engine's first choice is often already known.

steps.caption: Black to move. A known line: the usual recapture is 5...Nxd5. Model note: reason, Na5 attacks the bishop on c4 (checked); evidence, Stockfish 19 Lite at depth 16 rates Nxd5 at least 80 centipawns worse than the best move (checked); unproven, the lines after 6.Bb5+ c6.

steps.text: **What this app can check, and what it cannot.** Its items were checked offline with Stockfish 19 Lite, depth 16, one thread (roughly 16 half-moves). Nothing here can check that a move is new to theory: the Openings page holds online games, not master games. So 'new' here means rare at your opponent's rating. An engine score (100 centipawns is about one pawn) is evidence under those limits, not proof.

A **written justification** has three lines. The concrete reason: a capture, check or threat that the old move allows and yours stops. The evidence with its settings: engine, depth, centipawn gap. What remains unproven: deeper lines, untested replies. **Rule of thumb:** a gap of a few centipawns is not an improvement. If you cannot write the first line, you have an engine move, not a novelty.

title: Remember the forcing lines, understand the rest
outcomes: Tells a forcing line (exact recall) from a flexible position (understanding) by asking whether a natural move loses a lot or many moves work

Explains why spaced review fits forcing lines best

steps.text: Preparation has two jobs. **Exact recall** is for forcing lines, where one slip loses at once: you remember the move. **Understanding** is for flexible positions, where many moves work: you know the plan and the structure. More memorised moves is not better preparation; memory spent on flexible positions is wasted. First, sort two positions.

Real games show which lines are worth the memory. On the Openings page, after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Bc4, Black plays 3...Bc5 in 21% of games at 1100-1300 (869 of 4,100). The engine prefers 4.Nxe5, yet only 29% of White players take it in that band. The line is forcing, and each reply needs its own move. Watch it once.

steps.caption: White to move after 3...Bc5. A forcing line, with a different next move in each branch.

title: An opening is a route to a structure and its plans
outcomes: Explains that different move orders can reach one pawn structure, and that the structure suggests plans
Chooses a plan-consistent move for the Carlsbad, isolated-pawn and open-centre structures
Sees that the same pawn push can work in one structure and fail in another

steps.text: An opening is a route to a **structure**: the shape of the pawns. Pawns cannot go back, so the shape stays, and it says where pieces belong and which pawn pushes matter. Different move orders can reach the same structure. Learn a few structures and their usual plans, and many openings become one problem.

steps.caption: Route A. White's c-pawn is gone from the board and Black has no e-pawn.

steps.text: **Carlsbad:** White has no c-pawn, and Black has pawns on c6 and d5. White often pushes the queenside pawns (b4, then b5) to create a target on c6, or trades pieces. Black often repositions a knight toward the kingside or trades pieces. These are usual plans, not laws.

**Isolated d-pawn:** a pawn on d4 with no friendly pawn on the c or e file. Pawns cannot defend it, but it gives space and open lines. The owner usually keeps pieces on and aims them at the king. The other side adds pressure, blockades d5 and trades pieces. Tendencies, not laws.

steps.title: The same push in different structures

steps.text: **Open centre:** the central pawns are traded and files and diagonals are open. Speed and king safety count most. Put rooks on open files and develop before you attack. These are tendencies; check what the opponent's last move attacks first.

steps.text:
A **passed pawn** has no enemy pawn in front of it on its file or a neighbouring file. A **blockade** puts a piece on the square directly in front of it, so the pawn cannot advance.
**Rule of thumb:** the default blockader is a **knight**, because it loses no strength standing in front of the pawn. A queen there tends to be driven off; the king belongs in the endgame.

steps.text:
**Rule of thumb:** a blockade works when the blockading square is **safe** and the pawn is dangerous (passed, advanced or central). Check who attacks the square, above all pawns. A piece on a square an enemy pawn attacks will simply be taken.
It is a default, not a duty: if the pawn can be won, win it. A queen can blockade when nothing can hit it.

steps.text: A **pawn break** (or lever) pushes a pawn so that it can be exchanged for an enemy pawn. It opens a file or diagonal, or changes the pawn structure. It is also how you attack a chain of pawns: strike at the **base**, the pawn at the back that protects the rest. Judge a break by what it opens and who is ready to use it.

Count the defenders of the break square against the attackers, check that no pin punishes the move, and look at what the push uncovers: a pawn that leaves its square can open a diagonal or file for the opponent.
