steps.text: A **free centre pawn** is an enemy pawn on d4 or e4 (d5 or e5 if the enemy is Black) that none of your pawns attacks and that can advance. You have two answers. **Break** it with a prepared pawn move that attacks it, or **restrain** it: place pieces so that the square in front is covered, and wait. Neither answer always works.

steps.text: Both answers cost something. A break needs the pieces behind it: count the defenders of the break square against the attackers. Restraint takes several moves and ties pieces to their squares, so it is slow; that is a *rule of thumb*, not a law. Sometimes the break is not ready, and sometimes there is no free pawn at all. Check which case you are in.

steps.text:
Rooks are **connected** when they stand on one rank or file with no piece of either colour between them. Then each rook defends the other, and they can share a file. At the start the knights, bishops, queen and king are in the way, so connecting is usually the **last step of development**, not the first.
*Which pieces are in the way, and where can they go?*

steps.caption: White to move. Only the queen stands between the rooks on a1 and f1.

line.say: The queen leaves d1. Nothing stands between the rooks on a1 and f1 now: they are connected.
Black strikes in the centre. This changes nothing about the rooks.
One rook goes to the d-file. The rook on f1 still defends it, because nothing stands between them.

claims.statement: At the start the rooks are not connected.
After Qc2 they are connected.
After Rad1 the rook on f1 defends the rook on d1.

steps.text:
**Rule of thumb:** connect the rooks once your other pieces are out and nothing is pending. It is a step, not a goal.
Before you do, ask: *is any piece loose, mine or theirs? Is there a move that makes a threat?* Connecting can also wait on purpose, for instance when castling is delayed. And connected rooks on closed files do little until a file opens.

steps.title: Same position, one rook moved
steps.prompt: In the second position Black's a8 rook stands on d6. Does castling long, which connects White's rooks, still look best? Predict first, then check.
In the last positions, what did you check first: whether the rooks were connected, or whether anything could be attacked? Which should come first?

title: Converting an advantage: take, exchange or stay quiet
outcomes: Lists the kinds of move available when clearly ahead: take material, exchange pieces, make a threat, make a quiet move
Asks what the opponent's best reply would be before taking a pawn
Chooses among the kinds in positions the engine rates as clearly better, and names what the engine's line shows
Does not treat 'clearly ahead' as a reason to stop calculating

steps.text: When you are clearly ahead, the advantage has to be turned into something that cannot slip away. Your kinds of move: **take material**, **exchange pieces**, **make a threat** (a pawn push or piece move that attacks something), or play a truly **quiet move** that keeps his counterplay small. Before you choose, ask: after my move, what is his best reply? The strongest move is not always the one that wins the most.

steps.caption: White to move and clearly ahead. The rook can take the pawn on b7.

line.say: The rook takes the pawn and attacks the queen and the bishop.
The queen steps away.
The rook takes the bishop.

claims.statement: The engine rates the position at least 300 centipawns in White's favour.
After Rxb7 the rook attacks a7 and e7.
Rxb7 is the engine's best move.
Qxb7 is at least 300 centipawns worse than Rxb7.

steps.text: Which kind of move is best depends on the position, so this is a *rule of thumb* and not a recipe. Taking is often best when the capture is also the strongest line. An exchange can be best when it leaves an ending you can judge. A threat can be best when it forces a concession. A quiet move can be best when a capture would give him counterplay. Being clearly ahead still needs moves: check his forcing replies first.

steps.title: Take, threaten, wait or trade
steps.prompt: The engine rates all three positions as clearly better for the side to move. Predict which kind of move is best in each, then check.

Think of a game of yours where you were clearly ahead and the win slipped. Which kind of move (take, exchange, threaten or quiet) did you play, and what was your opponent's best reply at the moment you chose? Write the move and the reply.

title: Development: a lead you can spend
outcomes: Counts developed pieces on both sides before attacking
Explains why a sacrifice works against an undeveloped army and fails against a developed one
Decides when castling is urgent and when it can wait

steps.text:
Development is a lead you can spend. When your pieces are out and the enemy's are still at home, lines open in your favour and his king has few helpers, so a sacrifice that opens them can win.
Before you attack, **count the pieces in play on both sides.** The same sacrifice that wins against an undeveloped army loses against a developed one.

steps.caption: White to move. Black has played ...Bg4 and ...b5 but left the other pieces at home.

line.say: Bxf7+ strikes at the king, which has no developed helpers.
The king must take.
Check again: the king is dragged into the open.

steps.text: The attack is licensed by the lead, not by the sacrifice. Ask: **how many Black pieces are developed, and can his king find a safe square?** If he has a developed defender and a flight square, the sacrifice only loses a piece. A lead also fades: use it before the opponent catches up.

steps.title: Same sacrifice, one more defender
steps.prompt: Black has also played ...Nf6. Does Bxf7+ still work? Predict first, then check.

steps.text: Castling early gets the king safe and brings a rook into play. It matters most when the centre can open. When the centre is closed, castling can wait a move or two. Ask: **can the opponent open the centre now?**

steps.title: Same king, a different centre
steps.prompt: White's pawn is on e3 instead of e4. Is castling still the only good move? Predict first, then check.
Before you counted the developed pieces: how sure were you that the sacrifice worked? (low / medium / high)

title: Dynamic play: count the activity, not only the pawns
outcomes: Lists the damaged pawns (isolated, doubled, backward) of both sides
Counts the activity that may pay for them: open files and the moves of the main pieces
States whether the activity is enough, and labels the verdict as an engine rating, not a proof
Does not assume that damaged pawns mean a worse position without a count

steps.text: Damaged pawns (isolated, doubled, backward) are a long-term cost, but not an automatic verdict. Active pieces, open files and the initiative can pay for them. So keep two lists: his damage and your activity. A verdict from this count is a *practical* judgement; the engine's rating in this app is evidence under stated limits, not a proof.

steps.caption: Black to move. Black has 2 damaged pawns (g6, g7); White has none. Count Black's activity before judging: the queen on d8 has 8 legal moves; the knight on c6 has 6 legal moves; open files: e.

line.say: The engine's first choice at depth 16. The rating puts Black no worse than 0.2 pawns behind: the count favours the activity, not the pawns.

claims.statement: Black's isolated pawns: none.
Black's doubled pawns: g6, g7.
Black's backward pawns: none.
The open files are: e.
Black's queen on d8 has 8 legal moves.
Black's knight on c6 has 6 legal moves.
The engine rates the position at most +0.2 pawns for White, so Black is no worse than 0.2 pawns behind.
At depth 16 Qd7 is the engine's best move.

steps.text: Activity pays only while it can be used. A closed centre, a trade of your active pieces or one lost tempo can turn the count. *Rule of thumb:* damaged pawns without activity are a real problem; damaged pawns with open lines may not be. If neither side has damaged pawns, there is nothing to count. Compare the three positions below.

steps.title: Paid for, not paid for, nothing to weigh
steps.prompt: Predict which statement fits each position. In the second, a Black queen has moved from c6 to a8; the third is a different position. Then name the one change that flipped the verdict between the first two.

title: When the rule fails: test it with one change
outcomes: States a positional rule (rook to the open file, piece to an outpost) and the feature a position needs for it to hold
Compares a position where the rule gives a good move with one where a single change makes it fail
Says when the rule does not govern the position at all
Keeps a rule as a default with a condition, neither absolute nor discarded after one exception

steps.text: A rule of thumb is a default with conditions. "Put a rook on an open file" gives a good move in many positions and a poor one in others. To learn the condition, change one feature of a position that fits the rule and see whether the rule still gives a good move. One failure does not cancel the rule; it shows where its limit lies.

steps.caption: Black to move. The rule of thumb says: put a rook on an open file. Here it can be followed.

line.say: Rb2 follows the rule, and the engine rates it among its best moves. The rule works here.

claims.statement: The open files are: b, d.
The legal rook moves to an open file are: Rb1, Rb2, Rb3, Rb4, Rb5, Rb6, Rb7, Rbd8, Rfd8.
At depth 16 the accepted move (Rb2) is within 0.4 pawns of the best, and the best move is one of them.

steps.text: Keep each default with its condition: *take the open file, unless something else is more urgent, such as a capture or a threat*. Before you follow a rule, name what it assumes. The pair below differs by one feature, so the feature that licenses the exception can be named; the third position is one where the rule does not apply at all.

title: Trades: which piece goes, which stays
outcomes: Compares the pieces you give up and keep before trading
Chooses the trade that removes the enemy's most active piece
Checks the recapture before capturing

steps.text:
A trade changes two things: **the piece you give up** and **the piece you keep.** Before trading, ask what the enemy piece is doing for him (holding an outpost, attacking, defending) and what your recapture will look like.
Trading just because you can does neither job.

steps.caption: Black to move. Which trade is best?

line.say: The bishop takes the knight on c5.
White recaptures with the pawn.

steps.text: When two trades are possible, compare them. **Rule of thumb:** give up the piece that matters less, keep the one that fits your pawns and plans, and prefer the trade that removes his most active piece. Always look at the recapture before you take.

steps.title: Same target, a different piece takes
steps.prompt: Black could also take the knight with the bishop. Is 1...Bxd5 as good as 1...Nxd5? Predict first, then check.

title: Freeing moves: the break after the pieces
outcomes: Says which developing move should come before a planned pawn break in a given position
Checks the pieces behind a break (developed or still at home) before playing it
Tells a break that is ready from one that is premature when one piece has moved
Recognizes a position with no break at all

steps.text: A **freeing move**, usually a pawn break, offers an exchange of pawns to open lines. It helps the side whose pieces can use the lines. So the same pawn move can be good in one position and bad in another. Before you play a break, count which of your pieces still stand at home, and which pieces of his guard the squares the break aims at.

steps.caption: White to move. Both White knights are developed.

line.say: The pawn attacks d6 and f6 and offers an exchange.
Black takes.
White retakes. The pawn on e5 now attacks the knight on f6.

claims.statement: e5 is the engine's best move.
After e5 the pawn attacks d6 and f6.
After the exchange the pawn on e5 attacks f6.

steps.text: A break is ready when the pieces behind it are ready. As a *rule of thumb*, finish the development that stands next to the break before you push. Ask three questions: which of my pieces are still at home? Which of his pieces guard the squares the break opens? Does the move leave something loose? A break that opens lines for the opponent's developed pieces is premature.

steps.title: The same break, ready and premature
steps.prompt: In the first two positions White considers e4-e5; they differ by the position of one White knight. In the third, ask whether a break exists. Predict, then check.
In the silent positions, before you chose, which pieces did you check that were still at home? Write the position where a single piece changed your answer.

title: Good and bad pieces: now, and later
outcomes: Finds the worst-placed piece of each side by counting squares
Says why a piece is bad: hemmed in by its own pawns, shut out, or passive
Tells a bishop that is only temporarily bad from one that stays bad

steps.text:
A piece is **good** or **bad** by what it can do now: squares, targets, a useful job. Bad means few useful squares: hemmed in by its own pawns, shut out, or passive.
It can be bad *now* and good later. Before you give up on it, ask: **can it do a job where it stands? can it move with a threat? can I trade it for the enemy's best piece?**

steps.caption: Black to move. The bishop on c8 is shut in by its own pieces and pawns.

line.say: Black plays b6. The bishop on c8 now has two squares, b7 and a6.
White captures on d5. The bishop still has the same two squares.
Black recaptures. The pawn leaves e6 and light-squared pawns become fewer.
White moves a bishop. This does not change the bishop on c8.
The bishop reaches b7, but its own pawn on d5 still blocks the long diagonal.

claims.statement: The bishop on c8 starts with 0 legal moves.
Five of Black's eight pawns stand on light squares, the colour of the bishop.
After b6 the bishop on c8 has 2 legal moves.
After White's bishop move the bishop on c8 still has 2 legal moves.
After the exchange on d5, three of Black's seven pawns stand on light squares.
On b7 the bishop has 3 legal moves.
After the five moves Black's own pawn stands on d5.
On b7 the bishop attacks its own pawn on d5 but not e4 behind it: the long diagonal is blocked.

steps.text:
**Rule of thumb:** keep your own pawns off the colour of your bishop; this is well supported. The opposite advice, pawns on the colour of the enemy bishop, is only a hypothesis; the pawns may become targets.
A bishop hemmed in by pawns is bad only for now if one pawn move frees it. And the worst piece is not always the first to fix.

steps.title: Same pawn move, one pawn moved
steps.prompt: In the next position the f-pawn stands on e6, not f7, and Black plays the same pawn move, d6. Does the bishop get out? Predict first, then check.
In the last positions, before you moved, which piece did you name as the worst placed? Did you check what it could do where it stands before trying to move it?

outcomes: Lists the differences between the two sides from the board (files, bishops, outposts, pawns)
Chooses the one difference the next move can use
Says why a filled-in list is a start, not a verdict

steps.text: **An imbalance is a difference between the two sides.** Read the board for: pieces (a bishop pair, an outpost square), pawns (weak pawns, majorities), files (open or half-open), space (how many squares your pawns control in the other half), king safety. Write the list first. Then ask one question: **which difference can I use in the next few moves?** The list is where you start. It does not pick the move.

steps.caption: White to move. The list: the e-file is open, and Black owns both bishops.

line.say: Rce1: the rook takes the open file.
Black steps the bishop back. Black still owns both bishops.

claims.statement: The e-file is open.
Only Black has the bishop pair.
Rce1 and Rfe1 are the only rook moves to an open file.
The engine's first choices are the two rook moves.

steps.text: **A difference helps only if you can use it.** *Rule of thumb:* an open file is useful when a rook can reach it and nothing stops the rook; a bishop pair is useful when the bishops have open lines. The differences also pull against each other: one side has the file, the other the bishops. Read the facts first, then ask what the opponent can do about them.

title: Pawn majorities: the candidate and the kings
outcomes: Counts the pawns on each wing and finds the majority
Names the candidate and shows how a passed pawn arises by exchange
Sees that the first pawn move and the kings' positions can matter more than the count

steps.text:
A **pawn majority** is more pawns than the opponent on one wing (files a-d or e-h). Its job is to make a **passed pawn**. The pawn with no enemy pawn in front of it on its own file is the **candidate**; it usually leads and the others follow.
Only *healthy* pawns count: no tactics, no doubled or blocked pawns.

steps.caption: White has two pawns against one on the queenside. White to move.

line.say: The a-pawn has no Black pawn in front of it. It leads and offers an exchange.
Black takes on a6. Each side now has one pawn on the wing.
White recaptures. Black has no pawns left, so the pawn on a6 is passed.

claims.statement: White wins from the start position (tablebase, exact).
a6 keeps the win.
After Black takes, each side has one pawn on the queenside.
After White recaptures, Black has no pawns on the queenside.
After White recaptures, Black has no pawns on the kingside either.
After the exchange the pawn on a6 is passed.

steps.text:
**Rule of thumb:** the candidate leads, the middle pawn waits. It holds only while the majority is healthy and nothing else interferes. Counting is the first step, not the last: **king position and tempo can decide**.
Next: three pawns against two, the Black king far away, and two different first moves.

steps.prompt: Now White plays the middle pawn two squares, b4, instead of a4. Predict the result first, then check.

title: Manoeuvring: a target, a pivot and a route
outcomes: Names the target (a weak pawn that no piece attacks yet)
Finds the first step (the pivot) of a two-move route to a square that attacks it
Does not start a route when the engine rates the first step clearly worse, or when a capture wins material at once
Tells aimless moves from moves with a route

steps.text: To regroup against a weak pawn, name three things: the **target**, the **pivot** (a square your piece reaches first and passes through) and the **route** of each piece. Aimless shuffling is not manoeuvring: every move must bring a piece nearer a square that attacks the target. *Rule of thumb:* it works when the target can be attacked in two ways and your pieces have more room than his.

steps.caption: White to move. Black's pawn on d6 is backward, and no White piece attacks it. Target: d6. The engine rates Nc3 among its best moves; the later steps still have to be checked move by move.

line.say: The knight goes to c3: the pivot. From c3 it can reach b5, a square that attacks d6.

claims.statement: Black's pawn on d6 is backward.
No White piece attacks d6 now.
At depth 16 Nc3 is the engine's best move.

steps.text: A route needs time and safe squares. It fails when the pivot is controlled by the opponent, when he can use the time better, or when a tactic is on the board and no regrouping is needed. The app checks the squares and the engine's rating, not whether you have a plan. Compare the three positions below.

title: Obstructions: name what blocks the line
outcomes: Names the pawns or pieces that block a rook's file or a bishop's diagonal, for both sides
Is told that a piece in front of a passed pawn is a blockade, taught in another lesson
Counts attackers and defenders before trying to remove an enemy obstruction

steps.text: An **obstruction** is a pawn or minor piece that blocks the line of a rook, bishop or queen: a file or a diagonal. It can be the enemy's or your own. A **blockade** is different: a piece placed in front of a passed pawn to stop the pawn. To find obstructions, follow each rook, bishop and queen along its line until it meets the first man.

steps.caption: White to move. The black pawn on e5 and the knight on d5 stand on the lines of White's rook and bishop.

line.say: Nxe5: two white pieces attack the pawn and one black piece defends it.
Black takes back.
Rxe5: the rook recaptures; White has won a pawn and the rook now looks up the file as far as the bishop on e7.

claims.statement: Two white pieces attack e5.
One black piece defends e5.
The rook's line stops at e5.
The engine's first choice is Nxe5.

steps.text: *Rule of thumb:* an enemy obstruction is easier to remove than one of your own, because you can bring many attackers against it. **Count first:** attackers against defenders, including pieces that join after the first capture; the cheapest man should capture first. With more attackers, taking or exchanging the obstruction can open your line. Without them, leave it alone. An obstruction only troubles the side whose line it blocks.

steps.title: Same pawn, one more defender
steps.prompt: Working: the pawn is attacked twice and defended once. Failing: the same position with one more defender. Predict, then check. (A piece standing in front of a passed pawn is a blockade, taught in "Blockading a passed pawn: check the square".)

title: Open files: find the entry square
outcomes: Names the entry square before placing a rook on an open file
Checks whether a pawn or minor piece covers the entry square
Counts attackers and defenders before capturing a blocking pawn

steps.text:
An open file is a road, not a prize. A rook standing on it does nothing until it can **land** on a square in the enemy camp, best of all on the seventh rank, where pawns and the king are cramped.
Before you double rooks, ask: **which square will my rook land on, and can the enemy cover it?**

steps.caption: White to move. Follow the rook.

line.say: The rook lands on c7. No Black piece attacks that square.
Black makes room for his king.
The rook takes b7. White has won a pawn.

steps.text:
The plan works when three things hold.
**Your rook gets to the file first.**
**The entry square is not guarded by a pawn or a minor piece.**
**Something is waiting there:** undefended pawns, or a king with no room.
If the entry square is covered, landing there can cost you the rook.

steps.title: Same rook, one change
steps.prompt: Black's knight stands on e8 instead of h5. Does Rc7 still win a pawn? Predict first, then check.

steps.text:
Sometimes a pawn blocks the file. Count first: if it has fewer defenders than you have attackers, take it with your cheapest piece first.
If another pawn protects it, taking it may only lose material. Players then undermine it with a pawn lever or, rarely, give up material to open the file, but only when the landing square wins at once.

steps.title: Same pawn, one change
steps.prompt: Black's b-pawn stands on b7 instead of b6, so it protects c6. Does the knight capture still win a pawn? Predict first, then check.
Before you looked: what did you expect to be guarding the entry square in the last position? Was it a pawn, a minor piece, or nothing?

outcomes: Finds the piece with the fewest moves and says what cuts it off: its own men, or enemy pawns that attack every square it could reach
Tells a piece that is out of play from one that has plenty of moves
Checks what a freeing pawn move would cost before playing it
Does not treat a shut-in piece as lost, and does not free it at any price

steps.text: A piece is **out of play** when it can do little: its own men block it, or enemy pawns attack every square it could reach. A **trapped** piece is different: the opponent can win it. A piece out of play may stay on the board for a long time and be freed later. Ask: what cuts it off, and what would freeing it cost?

steps.caption: White to move. The bishop on d3 has no legal move: c4, e4, c2 and e2 all hold White's own men.

line.say: The c-pawn leaves c4, so the bishop gets c4, b5 and a6 at once. Black can take the pawn.
Black takes: White is a pawn down, yet the engine still lists c5 among the best moves.

claims.statement: The bishop on d3 has no legal move.
It attacks only c2, c4, e2 and e4.
A White pawn stands on c4.
A White pawn stands on e4.
A White pawn stands on c2.
The White queen stands on e2.
After c5 dxc5 the bishop has three legal moves.
c5 is among the engine's top moves.
After c5 three Black men attack the pawn on c5.
Only the bishop on e3 defends it.
After c5 the bishop on d3 sees c4, b5 and a6.
After c5 the bishop already has three legal moves, before Black takes.
White has four pawns on the queenside (files a to d).
After c5 dxc5 White has three queenside pawns instead of four: a pawn down.

steps.text: Out of play is not lost. A pawn lever or an exchange can often free the piece, but the price differs: the same lever can be free in one position and costly in another. As a *rule of thumb*, count the squares, then ask what the lever allows. The count is only a first test: a piece can also be out of play because it stands far from the action.

steps.title: Can b4 free the shut-in bishop?
steps.prompt: In the first two positions White's bishop on a2 is shut in by the pawn on b3, and the plan is b4. You see the first with its result, then predict the second. They differ by one Black pawn (on a6 or on a5). In the third, only the bishop's square differs.
Think of your last game. Which of your pieces did the least, and what cut it off: your own men or the enemy's pawns? Write one line, then say what freeing it would have cost.

title: Outposts: a square no pawn can reach
outcomes: Names the conditions of an outpost: protected, not attackable by a pawn
Checks the neighbouring pawns before planting a knight
Explains why a square a pawn can challenge is not an outpost

steps.text: An **outpost** is a square deep in the enemy half that no enemy pawn can ever attack. A piece planted there, usually a knight, is hard to remove and cramps everything around it. A pawn of yours one file over and one rank behind keeps it protected: e4 behind a knight on d5.

steps.caption: Black to move. Watch the knight.

line.say: The knight jumps to d4. The pawn on e5 protects it.
White has no pawn that can attack d4.

steps.text:
Before you plant a piece, check three things.
**Is it protected,** ideally by a pawn?
**Can an enemy pawn attack the square?** Pawns never move backward, so look at the pawns still standing on the neighbouring files.
**Is there something to aim at?**
If a pawn can chase the piece away, you only lose time.

steps.title: Same knight, one pawn different
steps.prompt: Only one Black pawn differs between the two positions. Can a Black pawn drive the knight away from d5? Predict first, then check.
Before you looked at the pawns: did you expect the knight on d5 to be safe? Which pawn did you check first?

title: Over-protection: when a point deserves a second defender
outcomes: Counts the attackers and defenders of a pawn and says whether a further defender is a developing move or only a lost tempo
Names the point that deserves extra defenders and a piece that can bring one while developing
Declines to add a defender to an ordinary pawn, or to a pawn nobody attacks
Labels the idea as practical, not proven

steps.text: **Over-protecting** means giving an important point more defenders than the attack on it needs. The idea comes from a master's writing and is *practical, not proven*. The point should be strong, central and under lasting pressure. The hope is that the defenders stay close to the point and keep their moves. For an ordinary pawn it is simply a lost tempo. In the examples here the extra defender is also a developing move, so the engine's agreement does not show that over-protection itself helps.

steps.caption: White to move. The pawn on e4 is attacked once, by the knight on f6, and defended once, by the rook on e1.

line.say: A second defender of e4 arrives, and the knight can reach f1 and g3 later.
Black develops.
The bishop defends e4 as well, and the pawn on e4 is defended three times.

claims.statement: One Black piece attacks e4.
One White piece defends e4.
After Nbd2 two White pieces defend e4.
After Nbd2, ...Bb7 and Bc2 three White pieces defend e4.
Nbd2 and Bc2 are the engine's two best moves.

steps.text: Ask three questions before adding a defender. Is the point strong and likely to stay under pressure? Does the defending piece keep useful moves where it stands? Is there a developing or active move that does the same job or more? As a *rule of thumb*, if the answer to the first is no, or if a developing or active move does the same job, leave the point alone.

steps.title: Same counts, different consequences
steps.prompt: In each position a move would add a second defender to a pawn. Predict whether it is among the engine's top moves, then check.

The master who proposed this idea mostly showed games he won, so those examples show it working and not how often it fails. The checks in this lesson are a handful of positions at one search depth. Name one point in your own games that you would try to over-protect, and one that you would not, and say why.

title: Passed pawns: blockade early, if you can arrive in time
outcomes: Names the blockade square in front of a passed pawn
Checks whether the blockader can arrive in time
Predicts win or draw when the defending king is in front or cut off

steps.text:
A **passed pawn** has no enemy pawn in front of it or on the files beside it, so only pieces can stop it. The usual way is a **blockade:** put a piece on the square in front of the pawn. In endings the king is the best blockader.
**Rule of thumb:** blockade early, with a piece that cannot easily be chased away.

steps.caption: White to move. The Black king is far from the pawn.

line.say: The pawn advances.
The Black king hurries towards it.
The pawn is one step from queening.

claims.statement: Exact result from the tablebase: White wins.

steps.text: The blockade is a strong default, not a duty: it works only if the blockader gets in front of the pawn in time. Ask: **can my blockader reach the square in time, and is it safe there?** In the next pair of positions only Black's king has moved.

steps.prompt: Only Black's king differs. Does the blockade still hold when the king stands on c8 instead of f8? Predict first, then check.

title: What a pawn move leaves behind
outcomes: Marks the squares a pawn move stops guarding and the pawns it leaves without a pawn protector
Checks which enemy pieces could use the new holes before pushing a pawn
Explains why a pawn move near the king is not automatically safer than a piece move
Tells a costly pawn move from one that is worth its price

steps.text: Pawns cannot move backward. A pawn move gives up the squares that pawn guarded, and the support it gave to neighbouring pawns, for the rest of the game. Before you push, name what it **stops guarding** and which pawns it **leaves without a pawn protector**. Then ask whether an enemy piece can use them.

steps.caption: Black to move. Think about what ...g6 would stop guarding.

line.say: The pawn leaves g7 for good. f6 and h6 become holes: no Black pawn can ever guard them.
The bishop goes to h6, one of those holes. A pawn can no longer challenge it there.

claims.statement: After g6, f6 and h6 are holes in Black's camp.
After g6 and Bh6 the white bishop stands on h6.
g6 is at least 0.8 of a pawn worse than the best move by the engine's count.

steps.text: A pawn move usually costs something when an enemy piece (a knight, a bishop of the right colour, a queen) can reach what it gives up. Sometimes the price is worth paying, for example to drive off an attacker. A pawn move near the king is not automatically safer than a piece move, and "never move those pawns" is no law either. Weigh cost against gain (a *rule of thumb*).

steps.title: When a pawn move has a price: Black's g6
steps.prompt: The first two positions are the same except for one White piece: the bishop stands on b1 in the first and on c1 in the second, and Black is thinking of g6 in both. You see the first with its result, then predict the second. The third is a different position: here White is thinking of g4.
Before you looked at the enemy pieces: when you saw a pawn move near a castled king, did you ask which piece could use the new holes? Write what you checked first.

title: Weak pawns: targets only if you can attack them
outcomes: Tests whether a weak pawn can be protected by a pawn before attacking it
Counts attackers and defenders on a backward pawn
Recognises a pawn that looks weak but is not a target

steps.text:
Isolated, doubled and backward pawns are called weak, but a weakness is only a **target** if you can attack it. Ask three things:
**Can a pawn of his protect it?**
**Can my pieces reach it,** for example along an open file?
**Do I attack it more often than he defends it?**
A pawn that fails these tests is just a pawn.

steps.caption: White to move. Black's d-pawn cannot be protected by a pawn.

line.say: The rook takes the backward pawn.
Black counterattacks.
White trades rooks first.
Black recaptures. White is a pawn up.

steps.text: A backward pawn is a target when **no pawn can protect it,** **your pieces can reach it** and **you outnumber its defenders.** If a neighbouring pawn can protect it, attacking wins nothing and can lose material. Doubled and isolated pawns follow the same test: weakness is a reason to look, not a reason to attack.

steps.prompt: Black's c-pawn stands on c7 instead of c5. Does Rxd6 still win a pawn? Predict first, then check.
Before you counted: how sure were you that the d6 pawn could be won? (low / medium / high)

title: A pin can last: four ways to meet it
outcomes: Names the four policies against a pinned knight and recognises the question (a flank pawn at the pinning bishop), ignoring and bringing up reserves in play
Checks whether the centre can be opened before asking again
Knows that more than one policy is often sound

steps.text: A pin need not be won at once; it can shape an opening. When a bishop pins your knight to the queen, you have four policies: **put the question** (a flank pawn attacks the bishop), **ignore** the pin and play in the centre, **bring up reserves** so the knight is no longer pinned, or **hold the choice** with a useful move and decide later. (No exercise in this lesson trains 'hold the choice'.)

steps.caption: Black to move. The bishop on g5 pins the knight on f6 to the queen.

line.say: h6 puts the question: the pawn attacks the bishop.
Bh4 keeps the pin. The bishop has answered the question.

claims.statement: h6 is the only pawn move that attacks the bishop.
The engine's first choice is h6.
The queen stands behind the knight.
The bishop on g5 attacks the knight.
e7 is empty, so the knight is pinned to the queen on d8.

steps.text: *Rule of thumb:* the question is good when the bishop's retreat leaves it few squares and the centre cannot be opened with profit, so the bishop cannot come back to life. It is bad when the centre can open, or when the pawn advance leaves your king facing a break. It does not always win a tempo, and it can weaken the side that asks.

steps.title: The second question: ...g5
steps.prompt: Black has played ...h6 and the bishop has gone to h4. Black now asks again with ...g5. In the second position the white f-pawn stands on f4; in the third, Black's queen is on d7. Predict each time, then check.
In the silent positions, which question did you ask first: 'is the piece pinned to something valuable?' or 'can the centre open if I ask?' Which one did you skip?

title: Plans: find the difference, check it is carryable
outcomes: Lists the differences between the two sides before choosing a plan
Sees that king position can outweigh an extra pawn
Checks whether the target of a plan is still there after one change

steps.text: A plan comes from the position, not from habit. List the **differences between the two sides**: material, king positions, open lines, weak squares. Ask which difference gives you something to aim at. Then check that the plan is **carryable:** do you have the pieces to execute it, and does the opponent have time to stop it?

steps.caption: Black to move. White is a pawn ahead. What are the differences?

line.say: Rxg2+: the rook and queen both aim at g2.
The king must take.
Check: the king is hunted and Black mates by force.

steps.text: The same attack needs the same target. If the key difference changes, the plan can vanish: ask **what is it aimed at, and is that still there?** Material is only one difference; king safety and open lines can outweigh it. Change one thing in the position and check whether your plan survives.

steps.prompt: White's king stands on b1 instead of g1. Does the rook sacrifice on g2 still work? Predict first, then check.

title: Better, worse or equal: the valuation sets the mode
outcomes: Labels a position better, worse or equal after listing the differences
Chooses a mode that fits the label: act, defend and restore freedom, or manoeuvre
Does not attack from a clearly worse position or sit still when clearly better
Checks a counter-attack before playing it

steps.text: Before you choose a plan, decide **who stands better**. Then match the kind of game to the label (a *rule of thumb*): if you are better, **play actively**, so the advantage is not wasted; if worse, **defend and restore freedom** by bringing pieces into play; if equal, **manoeuvre**: improve your worst piece and do not force matters. The label comes first, and it has to be honest.

steps.caption: White to move. Material is equal; the engine rates White clearly better [V], mostly on piece placement.

line.say: Nxd5 trades the knight for Black's centralised bishop.
Black recaptures.
Qc2: the queen joins and White stays active.

claims.statement: The engine rates the position at least 1.2 pawns for White.
The engine's first choice is Nxd5.

steps.text: The label is the hard part. Compare material, then king safety, then piece activity, and say where you are unsure. The mode is a default (a *rule of thumb*), not a law: a worse side may counter-attack, but a counter-attack has to be checked, and an attack from a clearly worse position is the most dangerous choice. An equal position often has several sound moves.

steps.title: Worse side: develop or raid?
steps.prompt: Black is clearly worse in the first two boards (same position). Board 1: the plan is to defend and bring a piece into play. Board 2: the plan is a queen raid. Predict whether the raid works, then check. Board 3 is a roughly level position: is there one clear move or several?
For each silent position, what label did you give it (better, worse, equal) before you chose a move? In which position were you least sure, and what would have made you sure?

title: Who goes, who stays: allocating pieces to a plan
outcomes: Asks of each attacking piece whether it also does a defensive job before sending it
Names a piece that must stay home and says what it blocks or guards
Says when there is no definite target to allocate pieces to

steps.text: **Allocation** starts with a target: a king, a weak pawn. Decide where the main blow falls, which pieces can go, and which are the minimum to keep at home. *Rule of thumb:* keep the defenders that also do other work (a knight on f3 can guard the king's side and the centre), and do not send everything. With no target yet, there is nothing to allocate.

steps.caption: White to move. The knight on f3 stands between Black's bishop on b7 and White's bishop on g2.

line.say: Ng5 sends the knight forward.
Black's bishop now attacks g2 and takes it.
Qxg2 recaptures. After the trade White's fianchetto bishop is gone and the engine rates Ng5 about 90 cp lower than g4 [V].

claims.statement: Black does not attack g2 now.
After Ng5 Black attacks g2.
Ng5 is at least 80 cp worse than the best move.

steps.title: Who stays, who goes
steps.prompt: Two questions about the board above: first, which white man is already doing a defensive job? Second, does sending the knight to g5 work? Then a different position: is there anything definite to allocate pieces to? Predict the last two, then check.

steps.text: A piece that looks like an attacker may be doing a defensive job (a shield): ask what changes if it leaves. Reserve only the necessary defenders, and recount, because one missed defender turns a winning attack into a losing one. *Rule of thumb:* count the pieces already aimed at the target plus those that can join with a threat next move; attack when that total beats the defenders. If not, improve your pieces first. The counting itself is taught in "Count before you attack: attack now, not yet, or no".

steps.prompt: Open one of your own games (My games) and pick a middlegame position where you attacked. Write down the allocation you used and the one you would use now.

title: Racing plans: the count in a pawn race, and what it leaves out
outcomes: Counts the moves each side's plan needs in a pawn race and says who arrives first
Remembers to ask who is on move
Checks whether a king can reach the pawn before trusting the count
Says that a count of moves does not apply when the pawns block each other
Reads the tablebase verdict shown after each item and compares it with his own count

steps.text: When both sides have a plan, count the moves each needs and ask who is on move. The side that arrives first usually wins. In a pawn race, count the moves a pawn needs to reach the last rank. A forcing reply can break the count: a king stepping into the pawn's path, or a check when a pawn queens. After each item, the answer shows the tablebase result.

steps.caption: White to move. Both kings stand behind their own pawns. White's pawn needs 3 moves, Black's needs 4.

line.say: White's pawn needs two more moves.
Black's pawn needs three more.
One more move.
Black needs two.
White queens first, with check along the eighth rank, so Black cannot queen.

claims.statement: With best play White wins.
White's pawn is on a5.
Black's pawn is on h5.

steps.text: The count is a *rule of thumb*. A king can break it. Draw a square with the pawn and its queening square on one side, as long as the pawn's moves still to go. If the enemy king can step into that square on his turn, he catches the pawn. Blocked pawns have nothing to count, and a queen that arrives with check can win a tempo. title: Prophylaxis: ask what he wants, then decide if it is real
outcomes: Names the opponent's freeing move in a given position by asking what he would play if you passed
Finds the quiet move that makes that break unattractive
Decides whether the break is real (the quiet move is clearly better than the alternatives) or not (several moves are equal)
Recognizes a position with no break to prevent

steps.text: **Prophylaxis** is a question you ask before you move: what does my opponent want to play next? If the answer is a real freeing move, a quiet move that makes it unattractive can be worth a tempo. It is not passivity. It is also not always needed: when his plan is not real, the question has a quick answer and you carry on.

Imagine you pass and look at his best move. Name what it would do: which pawn it attacks, which line it opens. Then find the quiet move that attacks that square or removes its support. As a *rule of thumb*, stop the break when, if he played it next move, you would lose a pawn or piece or be left cramped. If you would not, carry on with your plan. If he has no break, there is nothing to stop.

steps.prompt: Predict whether Black must deal with the break in the first two positions (they differ by one White knight) and whether the third position has any break to prevent. Then check.

title: A new valuation after every change
outcomes: Names the fact that changed after an exchange or a pawn move
Checks whether the old plan relied on that fact
Keeps the plan when nothing it relies on has changed
Picks a new plan from the new position when the old one is out of date

steps.text: A plan is a guess about one position. When the position changes (an exchange, a pawn move, a threat), the guess may be out of date. After each change ask two questions: **what changed?** and **did my plan rely on it?** If yes, make a fresh valuation, as a spectator would, and pick the plan again. If no, carry on. Changing plans when nothing changed wastes time.

For each reply, check those four things; even a far pawn can hit a piece (...c5 attacks a knight on d4). Ignoring a real change is *thinking inertia*; reacting to an irrelevant one wastes time.

title: Restraint: guard the square his pawn wants
outcomes: Names the square an enemy pawn would advance to and says which of your pieces attack it
Picks, from a piece's legal moves, the squares from which it would attack the break square
Tells apart a break that restraint can meet, one the opponent already supports, and a pawn that cannot advance
Does not spend a move watching a square when the engine's best move lies elsewhere

steps.text: **Restraint** means stopping an enemy pawn break before it happens. Find the pawn and the square it would advance to. If one of your pieces attacks that square, the push is no longer free; whether it costs him material depends on how many defend it. Nimzowitsch's order is a *rule of thumb*: restrain first, blockade next, destroy last. Free centre pawns have their own lesson, "A free pawn in the centre: break it or restrain it".

steps.text: Restraint costs a move, so first check that the break is **real**. Count the attackers of the break square for both sides (a *rule of thumb*, not a law). It fails when his advance is already supported, or when the pawn cannot move at all. Adding an attacker is also not automatically good: the engine's rating of the move still decides. title: The seventh rank: targets and a cut-off king

steps.text:
A rook on the **seventh rank** (the rank next to the enemy back rank) attacks pawns from behind, since they often stand on their starting squares, and it can keep the enemy king on the back rank.
To get there you need a safe **entry square** on an open file. Then look at what the rook can **attack** from the rank.

The White king comes forward to help the pawns.

Rxa7 keeps the win.
After Rxa7 the king on c8 still has only two squares.

steps.text:
**Rule of thumb:** a rook on the seventh is strong when it has **targets** (loose pawns, a king with no room) and the enemy king is **cut off** behind it. It is *not* a win by itself.
If the king can step out, or the target is defended, or there is nothing on the rank to attack, the same rook may do little. Check before you count on it.

title: Space: count the safe squares, then look for the lever

steps.text: In this app, **space** is counted from pawns only: the squares in the opponent's half of the board that your pawns attack. A white pawn on e5 attacks d6 and f6, so enemy pieces cannot use those squares without risk. A square is safe for a piece when no enemy pawn attacks it. More such squares usually leaves the other side's pieces fewer places to go. It is a count, not a judgement: it does not say the space is useful.

steps.text: **Rule of thumb, with conditions.** A space edge helps most when the other side's pieces really have few safe squares and no pawn can attack your space pawns. steps.text: **Rule of thumb, with conditions.** The minority attack tends to work when the exchange on c6 leaves a pawn to attack, rooks can use the c-file, the opponent has no quicker threat, and the pawn you push is not simply lost: count its attackers and defenders first. steps.text: A **pawn chain** is a line of pawns that defend each other diagonally. The **base** is the pawn at the back that no pawn defends; the **head** is the pawn at the front. This is the app's definition and it is simpler than book usage. Rule of thumb: a pawn lever against the base removes the support behind the rest of the chain, so play often goes there.

steps.text: **Rule of thumb, with conditions.** Attacking the base works best when the lever is supported and your pieces are ready; attacking the head leaves its defender where it is. The chain's owner has plans of his own, usually on the wing the chain points to (a rule of thumb this lesson does not test). For when a break is ready, see the lesson 'Pawn breaks: ready or premature?'.

steps.text: In this app, pawns are **doubled** when two or more pawns of one colour stand on the same file. steps.text: In this app, **hanging pawns** are two pawns side by side on the 4th or 5th rank, alone on their files and flanks, with no enemy pawn on their files. No pawn can defend them (a static weakness), yet they control squares and can advance (a dynamic strength). Rule of thumb: the plans are to hold them, advance one, or exchange them off.

steps.text: **Rule of thumb, with conditions.** Advancing tends to work when the advanced pawn gains something concrete, such as attacking a piece, and the pieces that could stop it can be hit. A well-placed enemy piece can make the same advance fail. This lesson tests the advance only; holding and exchanging are named, not drilled. Choosing the safest plan is not a rule.

Rule of thumb: the cramped side keeps its pieces flexible behind the sixth rank and waits for ...b5 or ...d5. The space side guards its space or strikes first.

steps.text: An **isolated queen's pawn** (IQP) in this app is a pawn on the d-file with no friendly pawn on the c- or e-file. title: The Maroczy bind: what it holds back, and what it costs

steps.text:
**Maroczy bind** (app's own definition): White pawns on c4, e4, none on the d-file; Black pawns on d6, g6, none on the c-file (colours may be reversed).
c4 and e4 attack d5, c4 also b5: Black needs preparation before ...d5 or ...b5. The price: d4 is a **hole**, a square no White pawn can attack now or by advancing, so an advancing pawn cannot drive a Black piece from it.

steps.caption: Black to move. Two White pawns (c4, e4) attack d5, and d4 is a hole in White's camp. Here Black's pieces are ready, so the break works.

line.say: d5: three attackers against three defenders, and the pawn on e6 can recapture.
White pushes e5; now only the pawn on c4 still attacks d5.

claims.statement: c4 holds the white pawn.
e4 holds the white pawn.
d6 holds the black pawn.
g6 holds the black pawn.
Open files: none. Half-open for White: d. Half-open for Black: c.
Two White pawns (on c4 and e4) attack d5.
No White pawn can attack d4 now or by advancing: d4 is a hole.

After d5, three Black pieces defend d5.
After d5, one Black pawn (on e6) attacks d5.
After d5 and e5, only the White pawn on c4 still attacks d5.

steps.text: **Rule of thumb, with conditions.** The bind holds while both breaks stay unready. The cramped side trades pieces and plays ...d5 or ...b5 when the square has enough defenders and a pawn can recapture; counting is the first check, not the whole answer. As pieces come off, it tends to get more room. The owner keeps c4 and e4: pushing either gives up part of the grip on d5.

title: Switching wings: can the heavy piece cross, and should it?
outcomes: Checks, from the legal moves, whether a rook or queen can change wings in one move

steps.text: A **switch of wing** has three parts. First a demonstration: a pawn advance or threat on one wing. Second, the opponent's pieces move across to meet it. Third, your own rooks or queen swing to the other wing, where fewer defenders now stand. In this lesson the kingside is files e to h. Rule of thumb: it works when your heavy pieces can change wings in a move or two and the opponent is slow to bring defenders back.

steps.caption: Black to move. Black has pushed a pawn to b4 on the queenside, where it attacks a3 and c3: that is the demonstration. White's king is on the kingside. The rook on a8 has not moved yet; the e-file is the first kingside file in this lesson (files e to h).

The pawn on b4 attacks a3 and c3.
White's king is on the kingside.
Rae8 is legal: the squares between a8 and e8 are empty.
At depth 16 Rae8 is among the engine's accepted moves (Rae8), all within 0.4 pawns of the best.

steps.text: **Rule of thumb, with conditions.** A swing needs mobile pieces and an opponent who is slow to answer. It fails if the path is blocked, if a pawn guards the landing square, or if you act on the first threat too early. The app can check legal moves and engine ratings but not the opponent's intentions. steps.text: Aim at what cannot get away. A **backward pawn** whose front square an enemy pawn controls cannot simply step forward, so you can bring more attackers. A piece **pinned** to its king cannot leave the line of the pin (the pin itself is taught in "Pins: cannot move, or should not move"). A piece that can move away is a poor target for a pawn kick: it moves, and the pawn that kicked it can never go back.

steps.text: A target is fixed only if it cannot step aside and the attack can bring more units than the defence. Before you push a pawn at a piece, ask where the piece goes. steps.text: A **transformation** changes what the position is made of: an exchange or a break turns one structure, or one kind of advantage, into another. A trade that leaves his pawns doubled or isolated can be worth it, but it has a cost, such as your bishop. Name both before you trade. title: Holes: squares your pawns can no longer guard
outcomes: Marks the holes in one side's camp: squares on its 3rd to 5th rank that none of its pawns can guard by moving forward
Names the enemy piece that could move onto a given hole
Checks that a piece can reach a hole and stay there, not only that the hole exists

steps.text: A **hole** is a square on your 3rd, 4th or 5th rank (counted from your own side) that none of your pawns can guard by moving forward, because pawns never move backward (a pawn changes file only by capturing). A hole is a weakness only if an enemy piece can **reach** it and **stay** there. It is a fact about *your* pawns; your opponent decides whether it matters.

steps.caption: White to move. Black has no e-pawn and his c-pawn stands on c5, so d5 is a hole in his camp.

line.say: The knight settles on d5. No Black pawn can ever attack it, and no Black piece attacks it now.

claims.statement: No Black pawn can ever attack d5.
After Nd5 no Black piece attacks the knight.
Nd5 is among the engine's top two moves.

steps.text:
Before you call a hole a weakness, ask three things.
**Can a piece reach it?** A knight can get there in time; a bishop only squares of its colour.
**Can it stay?** If an enemy knight or bishop attacks it, it can be traded off.
**Is there something to aim at from there?**
This is a *rule of thumb*: the more answers are yes, the more the hole matters.

title: A budget, not an equal share
outcomes: Splits a 15-minute game into an opening share, a middlegame share, an endgame share and a reserve that add up to the whole
Works out how many long thinks a middlegame share allows once routine moves are paid for
Tells a routine, a critical and a forced position apart and says whether a flat share is enough
Writes a budget to try in his next game and names the clock record that will check it

steps.text: A **time budget** is a plan for where the clock goes: a share for each phase, a reserve for the end, and room to think longer on the few moves that matter. **The same time on every move is not a budget**: it pays as much for a forced reply as for a decision. Every number here is a first guess to test against your own clock.

steps.prompt: A 15+0 game gives each player 15 minutes and adds nothing. Say the reserve is 2 minutes, the opening 3 and the endgame 3. The middlegame is moves 13 to 30, which is 18 moves. Work these out before you read on.

fields.label: Minutes left for the middlegame:
If each middlegame move costs a routine 10 seconds, how many one-minute thinks fit in what is left of the middlegame share?

steps.text: **Pay for routine moves first.** Give routine moves a small price and keep the rest of the phase share for critical moments, such as a tempting capture that may cost material (the pawn grab that loses a queen is an exercise in *How deep? Spend calculation where it pays*; here you only price it). Forced replies cost almost nothing. The prices (10 seconds, one minute) are a rule of thumb to adjust, not a measured optimum.

steps.title: How much of the budget does it deserve?
steps.prompt: Each position comes with the same budget: a routine move gets about 10 seconds. Decide for each: is it critical, so it needs extra from the pool, or routine, so the usual price is enough? A forced move, with one legal move, gets almost nothing; you meet one in the next exercises. Predict, then check.

steps.text: **When a budget works.** It works if you check it: compare your clock at move 12, move 30 and the end with the plan after each game. It fails when rigid: on a critical move, take the minute and pay it back from the share. It barely binds with a big increment (60+30 is about 120 seconds a move over 40 moves). Treat it as a rule of thumb.

steps.prompt: Sort each case. Does a time budget work, fail, or not apply? Choose, then save to see my answer. The answers are my judgement, not a measurement.

The plan says 10 seconds a move, and you play a tempting capture in 10 seconds without looking at the reply.

steps.text: **What the app does for you now, and when it stops.** The app does not time your games, and an imported game is not read for clock times. It keeps no record of time per move. So the budget lives on paper: write your clock at move 12, move 30 and the end. Once you can revise a budget from your notes, you do not need this page.

Time is a budget: **average time per move = time you have ÷ moves still to play.**

steps.text:
A result mixes your decisions, your opponent's decisions and luck. After a loss it is easy to blame yourself for everything or for nothing. A habit to try: judge the **decisions** (what you control) separately from the **result**.
This lesson makes no claim about feelings or about what raises ratings.

steps.text: A **process goal** is something you can do whether or not you win: 'run the safety scan on every move', 'write one unsure moment per game'. An **outcome goal** depends on your opponent: 'win', 'reach 1500'. Process goals are specific, in your control and checkable afterwards. They are a habit to try, not a proven method.

title: When you are worse: make it hard, and decide with a reason
outcomes: Lists the resources a worse position can have: a repeated check, a stalemate trick, a fortress, a move that sets a problem
Counts the opponent's winning replies to pick the move that sets the most problems among moves that all lose
Tests a swindle against the opponent's best reply before relying on it
Writes a play-on or resign decision with a reason and knows it is a judgement

steps.text: **Worse is not lost.** When you are behind, aim for the line that is hardest for the opponent, not the slowest loss. Your resources: a repeated check (a perpetual), a stalemate trick, a fortress, a move that sets a problem. Each has exact conditions and each can be tested against the opponent's best reply. Whether to give up the game is a different question: no source gives evidence, so we call it a judgement.

**Exact conditions.** A perpetual needs a safe check at every turn: count the king's squares. A stalemate trick needs two things: the stronger side has no better reply than taking the offered piece, and after that capture the weaker side has no legal move at all. A fortress needs its key squares held. A trap is worth setting only if the right reply costs you nothing (our rule of thumb).

steps.title: A fortress, and one change
steps.prompt: In the first position the defender holds a fortress. In the second, one thing is different. Predict the result each time, then check.

steps.text: No labels now. In each position the side to move is behind in material. Name the drawing resource it offers, or say there is none. Then check it against the opponent's best reply. The perpetual and the stalemate trick are taught in *Perpetual check: the draw you can force* and *Stalemate as a rescue*. The next two exercises are silent.
**Resign or play on?** Our working hypothesis, not a fact: play on while a resource exists and the game still teaches you something; resign when none is left.

steps.prompt: Choose a worse position from one of your own games. Write what you checked and what you decided. Keep a short log of ten such positions on paper or in your notes (the app does not track this yet), with the result, so that the working rule can be tested on you.

steps.text: Players often relax when they are ahead, and a classic slip follows: taking the first gain on offer without asking what the opponent threatens, or whether something stronger exists. **Feeling safe is a risk.** A habit to try: when you are ahead, run the safety scan and look at the opponent's best reply before every move, for ten moves in a row.

It costs seconds and does not mean refusing every gain: if the scan finds no threat, the capture is cleared, though a simpler way to stay ahead may be better. title: Why give material: the job a sacrifice does
outcomes: Names the job of a sacrifice (decoy, or removing a guard) and states the payoff that pays for it

Tells a sacrifice that fails from one that works after a single change to the position

steps.text:
A **sacrifice** gives up material for something you can name. Two jobs to look for first.
**Decoy:** lure a piece to a square where it hurts its own side.
**Remove a guard:** take or drive off the piece that guards a key square.
Some sacrifices do both jobs at once; say which one you would name first. No named job and payoff means you are guessing. Opening lines against a king: 'The Greek gift: when the bishop sacrifice on h7 works, and when it does not'.

Knight to f7 is checkmate.

steps.text:
**When a sacrifice holds.** The payoff must survive Black's best reply, including declining. *Rule of thumb:* count the king's flight squares and the pieces that can recapture before you give anything.
**When it fails.** One flight square, or one extra recapturing piece, can turn a mate into a lost queen.
**When it is not needed.** If the material can be won without giving anything up, win it that way.

title: Counting attackers and defenders
outcomes: Spots a pinned defender that cannot recapture

steps.text: You already know how to **count** a square from the lesson "Is this piece safe? Loose pieces and counting": list every piece that can capture there, start with your cheapest, and stop when carrying on would lose material. Here is that count once more, then the cases where it **lies**.

A black pawn recaptures.

The rook takes the knight. White has won two pawns and a knight for a pawn and a knight.

steps.text:
A count is only as good as its pieces.
**Order matters.** With the same numbers, a cheap piece that captures first can win what an expensive one would lose.
**Every counted piece must really be able to capture.** A pinned piece cannot recapture if that would expose its king, and a piece with two jobs may be needed elsewhere.

title: Counting what can arrive
outcomes: Lists the pieces each side can bring to a pawn's square with one move, and counts again

steps.text:
Counting the attackers and defenders of a square tells you the position **now**. A pawn you push, or one that stays where it is, is also reached by pieces that **arrive**.
So count twice. First count what attacks and defends the square. Then list the pieces of each side that can move to a square from which they attack or defend it, one move each, and count again.

White brings a second defender: the knight moves to c3. Two against two.
Black takes first with the knight, its cheaper attacker.
The knight takes the knight.
Black could take again with the rook.
The rook takes the rook. Black took a pawn and a knight; White took a knight and a rook.

steps.text:
Three conditions for the second count.
**The target stays.** A piece whose side is to move can step away.
**The arrival is effective.** Not boxed in, and not attacked on its landing square by a piece of lower counting value.
**It arrives in time.** **Rule of thumb:** two-move arrivals usually come too late.
Treat the count as a first estimate: a bigger threat can pull a defender away.

title: Five ways to meet an attack
outcomes: Names the five ways to answer an attack (move, defend, capture, block, counterattack) and uses the first four to save a piece
Saves an attacked piece by a named way, and by any way when none is named
Checks that the chosen way still works against that attacker, and that it leaves nothing else loose

steps.text:
When one of your pieces is attacked and nothing defends it, you have five kinds of answer.
**Move** it. **Defend** it. **Capture** the attacker. **Block** the line (only against a bishop, rook or queen). **Counterattack** with a bigger threat of your own.
List them before you choose. A counterattack works only if your threat is bigger than theirs, so as a rule of thumb look at the first four first.

steps.caption: White to move. The black rook attacks the knight on d4 and nothing defends it. Two of the five answers are open here.

line.say: Defend it: the bishop now guards d4.

claims.statement: The knight on d4 is attacked and nothing defends it.
After Be3 the engine line does not lose material for White.
The knight could also move to eight squares.

steps.text:
An answer must pass two checks.
**Does it stop the attack?** Defending fails when the attacker has a lower counting value than the attacked piece (a rule of thumb): a pawn takes a defended knight, and you lose a knight for a pawn. A far-away move does nothing unless it threatens more.
**Does it leave something else loose?** A defender that moves can leave the piece it guarded loose.

title: Real threats and fictitious ones
outcomes: Says whether an attack on a piece is a real threat
Names the reason when it is not: a defender, a pinned attacker, or a bigger loss behind the capture
Says that a fictitious threat can become real when the reason goes away
Says 'no threat' when nothing is attacked at all

steps.text:
An attacked piece is not always in danger. A threat is **real** if the capture gains something against best defence. It is **fictitious** if the capture fails. Three common reasons: the piece is defended and the attacker has a higher counting value; the attacker is **pinned to its king** and may not capture; the capture would let you win something bigger.
Ask before you react: **what happens after the capture?**

line.say: Suppose Black takes the bishop.
The pawn takes back. Black has given a rook for a bishop (counting values 5 and 3).

claims.statement: One black piece attacks the bishop.
One white piece defends the bishop.
If Black takes, the engine line leaves Black at least 2 behind.

steps.text:
A fictitious threat is fictitious **for a reason**, and the reason can end. A pin lifts when the king steps away. A defender can be driven off or traded. Forget it, and the threat may be real a few moves later.
**Rule of thumb:** check the capture first. If it fails, do not spend a move on it now, but watch for the reason to end.

title: Loose pieces: what can be taken for free?
outcomes: Names the loose pieces of either side
Takes a loose piece, the one with the higher counting value first
Checks for a far-away defender before calling a piece free
Says when there is nothing to take

steps.text:
Remember: a piece is **loose** when an enemy piece attacks it and none of its own side defends it. The enemy can take it for free. Lichess calls such a piece a hanging piece.
Two habits stop most beginner losses. Look at their pieces for loose ones. Then look at your own, after every move your opponent makes.

steps.caption: White to move. Which black piece is loose?

line.say: The rook takes the knight. No black piece defends d5, so nothing recaptures.
Black has lost a whole knight for nothing.

claims.statement: Only the knight on d5 is loose.
Rxd5 wins the knight.

steps.text:
A loose piece is free only on conditions.
**Count every defender**, including pieces that guard from far away along a file or diagonal.
**Ask what the capture costs.** A piece that has a defender is not free: if the defender can recapture, you may lose more than you win.

title: What did their last move threaten?
outcomes: Names what an opponent's last move threatens: a capture, a mate, or a fork

Says when the last move threatens nothing

steps.text:
After your opponent moves, ask first: **what does that move threaten?** Imagine they get a second move in a row. Could they win a piece, give mate, or fork? Look at what their piece now attacks and what it has just uncovered.
If the answer is 'nothing', you are free to follow your own plan.

steps.caption: Black to move. White has just played ...Re1. What is the threat?

line.say: Black ignores the threat and plays an unrelated move.
...Re8 is checkmate: the pawns shut the king in and nothing covers e8.

claims.statement: White threatens Re8 mate.
No black piece covers e8.

steps.text:
A threat is real only if carrying it out works. Ask:
**What would they take or attack?**
**After my recapture, do they gain?** A rook that takes a pawn-defended bishop loses material.
**Can they really play it?** A covered square or an escape square for my king can cancel it.
Sometimes the honest answer is: no threat.

title: Diagnose: which kind of mistake, and how do you know?

steps.text:
When you lose material, ask which box it belongs in.
**Not seen:** you never looked at the reply.
**Seen but miscalculated:** you looked and the count was wrong.
**Misjudged:** the count was right, your verdict on the position was wrong.
**Time pressure:** the clock decided.
The label is tentative: only the player knows what happened.

Different boxes may need different practice: not seen suggests a scan habit; miscalculated suggests practice with lines and counting; misjudged suggests comparing positions; time pressure suggests a clock plan. This pairing is a hypothesis to test, not a proven rule.

**An error log** lists each mistake with the game, the clock and a box. A diagnosis is a claim the log can test. outcomes: Designs a two-way comparison of training methods that changes one thing and keeps the rest fixed

steps.text: An **experiment** changes one thing and keeps the rest the same, so a difference can be blamed on the change. *Example:* practise forks **blocked** (all forks in a row) for two weeks, then forks **interleaved** (mixed with other themes) for two weeks, same minutes, with a check on new mixed positions after each. Two good sessions prove nothing. You need a measure, a check on positions you did not practise, and a decision rule written *before* you look.

In a block of forks you know the idea before you look; a **fair check** does not tell you. Rules of thumb: (1) positions you did not practise, not a mirror of one; (2) no idea named; (3) some positions where the practised idea fails, or 'always fork' scores full marks; (4) the same check for both methods. Compare two methods on one skill, not forks against pins; the order can also fool you (by the second fortnight you know more). Four silent positions follow as a tiny check.

A start of 3 of 8 and a check of 6 of 8 sounds like a doubling, yet the ranges overlap. 'Cannot tell' means not enough data, not 'no effect'. A plan that shows nothing, or goes down, is still data.

steps.text: An **investigation** starts with a claim you can name, with its source and year: a book, a video, or a 'rule of thumb' in these lessons. Turn it into a question a test could answer. What would I see if the claim is true, and what would show it false? Pick a tool, write its **limits**, and look for a **failing look-alike**. Checking an old claim counts as research; a novelty is not required.

steps.text: **A worked question.** Claim (made up here, so no source or year): a move that scores well on the Openings page must be sound. If so, moves with equal results should be about equally sound. Data (September 2026 online games, band 1300-1500) after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.d4 exd4: 4.Nxd4 (10,125 games) White won 53%, drew 4%; 4.Ng5 (2,519 games) won 53%, drew 2%. A draw counted as half a win gives 54.7% for both. Now ask the engine.

steps.caption: White to move after 3...exd4. Written beside this result: tool Stockfish, depth 16, one position; data from the Openings page, September 2026 sample, band 1300-1500. At depth 16 the engine ranks 4.Nxd4 first and rates 4.Ng5 at least 1.5 pawns lower. Failing look-alike: 4.Ng5 is a common move (14% of games here) that wins as often as 4.Nxd4 (53% each), yet it is the move the engine rates lower.

steps.text: **What each tool can and cannot show.** *Openings page:* what players of a band chose and how those games ended (one month, online); not why, and not strength. *Engine:* a fixed-depth rating of one position; not what people will do. *Your games:* real mistakes, but few. *Tablebase* (seven pieces or fewer; none in this app): exact for each position, so one position is a lookup, not research; a claim about many positions takes many lookups. steps.text: A conclusion is worth keeping when the test could have failed, the result sits beside its tool, sample, depth and band, and one **failing look-alike** is named. It breaks when you keep only the cases that agree, when the sample is tiny (a **rule of thumb**: under about 30 games in a band is noise; the Openings page hides such results), or when a lookup would have answered. A result that contradicts the source is a finding.

title: Back-rank mate, and luft as the cure
outcomes: Finds a back-rank mate
Tells a mate from a check when the king has luft or a guard covers the square
Sees the back-rank threat against his own king
Gives his own king luft with a pawn move

steps.text:
A **back-rank mate** is a check along the first or last rank against a king that is shut in by its own pawns. It works when three things hold: the king has **no escape square**, nothing can **capture** the checking piece, and nothing can **block** the line.
Take one away and it is only a check.

steps.caption: Black to move. Black's rook stands on the open e-file.

line.say: The rook checks along the back rank. The pawns cover the king's escape squares.

claims.statement: ...Re1 is checkmate.
No white piece covers e1.

steps.text:
The cure is **luft** (German for air): an escape square for the king. A pawn move in front of the king, such as h3 or h6, is usually enough. A piece that guards the back rank works too.
Look at your own back rank as well as your opponent's.

steps.title: One pawn move changes everything
steps.prompt: The h-pawn stands on h6 in the second position.

title: Clearance: step aside with a threat
outcomes: Finds the vacating move that carries a threat when told to clear a line
Checks what the cleared piece attacks once the line is open
Rejects a vacating move that has no threat, or that opens a line leading nowhere

steps.text:
A **clearance** is a move that takes a piece off a square or a line so that another piece can use it. It usually works only when the vacating move **carries a threat of its own**, such as a check or a capture: the opponent must answer it and has no time to cover what you opened.
Opening a line is not enough by itself.

steps.text: A forced mate is found by **listing**, not by hoping. List every check. For one check, list every reply: take the checking piece, block the line, or move the king. The check starts a **mate in two** only if you have a mating move against *every* reply. Here we test checks only: if every check fails, a quiet first move may still mate (next lesson).

steps.text: **Why the list matters.** A check can fail in three ways: the defender takes the checking piece, a block spoils your next move, or the king has a step you did not count. *Rule of thumb:* before you call a check a mate in two, try to take the checking piece with each enemy piece, king included. A capture is fine only if you still have a mating move after it.

steps.text: When no check works, look for a **quiet move**: not a check, but a threat of mate that no reply can meet. Search in this order: every check, then captures next to the king, then quiet moves. For a quiet move ask: how many moves does the king have? Can the defender check, or take my attacking piece? Does every reply allow mate? This order is a *rule of thumb*: it saves time and proves nothing.

steps.text: **Two ways a quiet move fails.** First, a counter-check: the defender gives check, a check must be answered at once, and the mate never comes. Second, one extra defender covering the mating square. A threat of mate is not a mate: it counts only if every reply, every check included, still loses. *Rule of thumb:* after your quiet move, list the defender's checks and captures first.

title: Perpetual check: the draw you can force

steps.text: A **perpetual check** is a series of checks that the king cannot escape, so the same position keeps returning. When a position occurs three times, a player can claim a draw. When you are worse, a perpetual can save half a point. It needs every reply to lead back into more checks, so **test the king's squares** first.

steps.caption: White to move. Black is ahead (a queen and three pawns against a queen), so White looks for checks.

No black piece attacks the queen on f7.
After Qxf7+ Kh8 Qf8+ the king on h8 again has exactly one legal move (h7).
After five moves the queen is on f7 again.
And the black king is on h7 again.

steps.text:
Three tests before you rely on a perpetual.
**Where can the king go?** Count its flight squares after each check.
**Can the checker be captured, or the check blocked?**
**Is the draw really your best result?** If another move wins, or the perpetual is not there, a draw may be a mistake. *Rule of thumb:* take the perpetual only when the alternatives are worse.

title: Pins: cannot move, or should not move
outcomes: Tells an absolute pin (no legal move) from a relative pin (legal but costly)
Wins a pinned piece by attacking it again
Checks that something valuable really stands behind the pinned piece
Tells a pin from a fork

steps.text:
A **pin** attacks a piece that cannot, or should not, move, because a more valuable piece stands behind it on the same line.
In an **absolute** pin the piece behind is the king, so moving the pinned piece is illegal. A pinned piece is easy prey: it cannot run away from a second attacker.

steps.caption: White to move. The black bishop on e6 stands between the rook and the king.

line.say: The pawn attacks the bishop. It is pinned and cannot leave the e-file.
Black moves the king, but the bishop is still attacked.
The pawn takes the bishop. White has won a bishop for a pawn at least.

claims.statement: f5 wins the bishop along the engine line.
The rook on e1 attacks the bishop.

steps.text:
Two kinds of pin.
**Absolute:** the king is behind. The pinned piece has no legal move.
**Relative:** something valuable, but not the king, is behind. The piece may legally move, but then it loses what stood behind it.
'Cannot move' and 'should not move' differ. A **fork** is one piece attacking two targets; a pin needs a line with something behind.

steps.prompt: In the second position the king stands on d8.

steps.text: Some pins win nothing at once. A pinned piece stays tied to its square and is a poor defender, which can shape play for many moves. Whether that matters is judged case by case, and later strategy lessons return to it.
