title: The quiet move: no check, no capture, still decisive
outcomes: Recognises a quiet move: no check, no capture, yet decisive
Finds the quiet move when told there is one
Checks the opponent's free replies (checks and captures) before trusting a quiet move
Prefers a forcing win when one exists

steps.text: Not every winning move is a check or a capture. A **quiet move** gives no check and takes nothing, yet it prepares a threat the opponent cannot meet, or it removes their last defence. Look for one when the forcing moves have run out. It is a move to find, not one to play by habit.

steps.caption: White to move. Look for a move that is neither a check nor a capture.

line.say: Rh1: no check, no capture. The rook lines up behind the queen, so Qxh7 would be mate.
Black has no defence that works; the engine finds this best.
The queen takes on h7 with checkmate.

claims.statement: Rh1 is legal.
The rook goes to an empty square: no capture.
No white piece attacks the king on h8 after Rh1: no check.
Rh1 forces checkmate in two.
Rh1 is the engine's first choice.

steps.text:
A quiet move gives the opponent a free move. Before you play one, ask:
**Does the opponent have a check or a capture that wrecks it?**
**Does a forcing line already win?** If so, play that; a showpiece is not a better move.
*Rule of thumb:* look at checks, captures and threats first, then at quiet moves.

steps.title: Does the quiet move still work?
steps.prompt: The first position is a quiet move that wins. In the second, a pawn has moved so that Black gets a strong reply. In the third, a pawn gives White a forced mate. Predict, then check.
When you looked for the quiet move, did you first check what the opponent could do with a free move (a check or a capture)? Which of the two was easier to forget?

fields.label: Did you check the opponent's free replies before choosing?
Which was easier to forget?

title: Attacking the defender: remove, deflect, decoy, overload
outcomes: Finds the capture that removes the only defender
Tells removal, deflection, decoy and overload apart
Counts the defenders and their jobs before attacking one
Says when a second defender or a capturing piece defeats the idea

steps.text: A defended piece is only safe while its defender can do its job. Attack the defender and the piece falls. There are four ways: **remove** it by capturing it, **deflect** it by forcing it to move, **decoy** it by luring it to a bad square, **overload** it by giving it two jobs.

steps.caption: Black to move. The white queen on e4 is defended by the king on e3.

line.say: The rook offers itself with check.
The king takes the rook and leaves e3.
The queen takes the queen with check.

claims.statement: ...Re2+ followed by ...Qxe4+ wins material along the engine line.
Only the king on e3 defends the queen on e4.

steps.text:
Before you attack a defender, count.
**Is it the only defender?** A second defender ends the idea.
**What are all its jobs?** An overloaded piece cannot keep two.
**What stands on the square after the exchanges?** Recount before you commit.

steps.title: A second defender
steps.prompt: A white pawn on f2 now guards g3 as well.
When a piece looked defended, did you list every job of the defender before you attacked it?

title: Skewers: the king moves, the piece behind falls
outcomes: Finds a skewer when told to look for one
Checks that the front piece cannot capture the attacker
Checks that taking the piece behind gains material
Says when a check lines up nothing

steps.text:
A **skewer** is a pin in reverse. You attack a valuable piece that has to move, and the piece behind it on the same line is left to be captured.
The commonest form is a check: the king must step aside, and what stood behind it falls.

steps.caption: Black to move. The white king stands in front of the knight on a2.

line.say: The bishop checks the king along the diagonal. The knight stands behind it.
The king must move out of check.
The bishop takes the knight.

claims.statement: ...Bd5+ followed by ...Bxa2 wins the knight.

steps.text:
Before you skewer, ask:
**Can the front piece capture my piece?** A king next to your bishop takes it unless it is defended.
**Does taking the piece behind gain material?** If it is defended and its counting value is no higher than your attacker's, you only trade.
Then check that nothing can step in between.

steps.title: The skewering piece can be taken
steps.prompt: Only the white rook has moved: from d1 to g1.
Before you played a check, how sure were you that the piece behind the king could be won? (low / medium / high)

title: Stalemate as a rescue
outcomes: Finds the sacrifice that forces a stalemate when told to look for one
Counts the legal moves left to the side that would be stalemated
Sees that a spare pawn move, or a king with room to move, ends the trick
As the stronger side, avoids the move that stalemates

steps.text:
In **stalemate** the side to move has no legal move and is not in check. The game is a **draw**: neither side wins.
So a side that is clearly losing can sometimes save the game by giving up a piece, usually with check, so that the capture leaves it with no legal move. The stronger side must check, before each quiet move, that the opponent still has a legal move.

steps.caption: Black to move. White has a queen, Black only a rook, and Black's king on c8 has no free square.

line.say: The rook goes to a7 with check, next to the white king.
The white king takes the rook. Black has no legal move and is not in check: stalemate, a draw.

claims.statement: With best play the position is a draw for Black (tablebase).
After Ra7+ the position is a draw (tablebase).
Rc7 loses (tablebase).
The black king has no legal move even now.
The rook on a7 gives check to the king on a8.
After Kxa7 the black king still has no legal move.
After Kxa7 nothing attacks the black king.

steps.text:
**When it works:** the capture is forced, and afterwards your side has no legal move and is not in check. That usually needs your king boxed in, often on the edge or in a corner, and no pawn or piece able to move.
**Check:** if your side has any legal move left, there is no stalemate. Count your own legal moves after the capture.

steps.title: Same sacrifice, one change
steps.prompt: Same position, one change: Black has an extra pawn on a7. Predict, then check.

When you were losing, did you check whether giving up a piece would leave your side with no legal move? When you were winning, did you count the opponent's legal moves before each quiet move? Where did you nearly stalemate a won position, or miss a draw?

title: Trapped pieces, and pieces that are only cut off
outcomes: Counts the escape squares of an attacked piece and says which are covered
Wins a trapped piece by attacking it
Tells a trapped piece from one that is only cut off

steps.text:
A piece is **trapped** when it is attacked, or can be attacked, and every square it can go to loses it. Knights on the rim and bishops that grabbed a pawn are the usual victims.
To trap a piece, count its escape squares and ask which of them you cover.

steps.caption: White to move. The black knight stands on the rim.

line.say: The pawn attacks the knight. Its squares b3 and c4 are covered and b7 and c6 are taken.
Black makes some other move.
The pawn takes the knight.

claims.statement: b4 wins the knight along the engine line.

steps.text:
Trapped is not the same as cut off. A piece that is **cut off** from the action still has a safe square, so you cannot win it. Before you attack, ask:
**Which squares can it reach?**
**Which of them do I cover?**
**Can it capture something, or can its friends help?**

steps.title: Trapped or only cut off?
steps.prompt: In the second position the white pawn stands on d2, not d3.
When you counted escape squares, did you check each one for a defender or a counter-attack, or only whether it was empty?

title: Underpromotion: when a knight or rook beats the queen
outcomes: Finds the promotion to a knight that gives check and attacks a second piece
Chooses a rook or a knight where a queen would stalemate
Checks the queen promotion first and says why it fails
Says when the queen is simply right

steps.text: When a pawn reaches the last rank, you choose its new piece. The queen is the usual choice because it is strongest. Sometimes another piece is better. A **knight** can give check and attack a second piece at once. A **rook** can win where a queen would leave the opponent with no legal move and no check: **stalemate**, a draw. Choosing a weaker piece on purpose is **underpromotion**.

steps.caption: White to move. Black has a queen on d7; the pawn on b7 is about to promote.

line.say: Underpromotion: a knight. It gives check to the king on a6 and attacks the queen on d7.
The king must move. Nothing can capture the knight on b8.
The knight takes the queen. The tablebase says White wins this position.

claims.statement: b8=N is legal.
A knight on b8 attacks a6 (the king) and d7 (the queen).
No black piece can capture a knight on b8, so the king must move.
White wins this position (tablebase).
Promoting to a knight keeps the win (tablebase).
Promoting to a queen loses (tablebase).

steps.text:
Check the queen first. Ask two questions.
**Does the queen promotion fail?** It might stalemate, or a knight's check and fork might win more.
**Does a knight on that square give check and attack a second piece?** As with any fork, ask whether the knight can be captured and whether the second target is worth taking.
*Rule of thumb:* the queen is the default. These questions find the exceptions.

steps.title: Does the knight still fork?
steps.prompt: In the second position Black's rook has moved from d7 to b7. In the third, no pawn can promote. Predict, then check.
Which part is least clear: seeing the knight fork, seeing the stalemate, or deciding that the queen is simply right?

title: X-ray and batteries: the piece behind joins in
outcomes: Counts attackers and defenders of a square including the pieces behind
Finds the capture sequence in which the rear piece joins in
Checks that the front piece is free to capture before counting on the battery
Tells a battery from a lone piece with nothing behind it

steps.text:
Two of your pieces on one line form a **battery**. The rear piece attacks, or defends, *through* the front one: once the front piece captures or moves away, the rear piece joins in. This is called an **x-ray**.
When you count attackers and defenders, include the pieces behind. Two rooks on a file are two attackers, not one.

steps.caption: White to move. The bishop on b1 stands behind the queen on d3, on the same diagonal as h7.

line.say: Qxh7 is checkmate. The king cannot take the queen, because the bishop behind it guards h7.

claims.statement: Qxh7 is checkmate.
Only the king attacks h7.
Before the capture the bishop does not reach h7: the queen is in the way.
After the queen has gone to h7, the bishop guards it.

steps.text:
**When it works:** the front piece can capture and leave the line, and the piece behind moves along that line. **Rule of thumb:** count attackers and defenders including the pieces behind, cheapest capture first, and remember that either side may stop trading.
**When it fails:** the front piece is pinned and cannot capture, or nothing stands behind it, so there is only one attacker.

steps.title: Same battery, one change
steps.prompt: Same position, one change: a black bishop stands on b5 instead of b7. Predict, then check.
In the silent positions, how many attackers and how many defenders did you count on the key square, including the pieces behind? Did you check whether the front piece was free to capture?

title: In-between moves: a check or capture first
outcomes: Asks, before a capture or recapture, whether a check or capture can be played first
Finds the in-between check or capture when told one exists
Re-counts the exchange to see that the original capture still wins what was expected
Recognises a position where the plain recapture is simply best

steps.text:
An **in-between move** (German: *Zwischenzug*) is a forcing move you play *before* the reply your opponent expects, such as the recapture. It is usually a **check**, which the opponent must answer, or a **capture**.
The question to ask before any capture or recapture: **is there a check or capture I can play first, and does my original capture still work afterwards?**

steps.caption: White to move. The pawn on c3 attacks the rook on d4, and Black's bishop on a6 attacks the white rook on b5. The expected move is to take on d4.

line.say: The attacked rook moves with check along the c-file. Black has to answer the check first.
The king steps aside. The white rook has left b5, so the bishop can no longer take it there.
Now the pawn takes the rook on d4. Along the engine line White gains at least five points of material.

claims.statement: The engine's best move is Rc5+ (depth 16).
Along the engine line White gains at least five points of material.
Taking at once with cxd4 is at least 600 centipawns worse (engine).
Black's bishop on a6 attacks the rook on b5.
The pawn on c3 attacks the rook on d4.

steps.text:
**When it works:** the in-between move forces a reply, and afterwards the capture you wanted still wins what you expected. **Rule of thumb:** look at checks first, because the reply is forced.
**When it fails:** for example when a pawn defends the target, so the follow-up capture wins nothing. After the forcing move, count the exchange again, and ask whether the opponent has an in-between move of their own.

steps.title: Same exchange, one change
steps.prompt: The black rook on d8 and the white rook on d1 face each other on the d-file. In the next position a white pawn stands on f4 instead of f2. Predict, then check.

In the silent positions, what did you expect your opponent to do next, and did you check that your capture still worked after your forcing move? (The practice puzzles carry Lichess's automatic theme label, which is not always an exact fit for this lesson.)
